item.title: Cold wave advisory set to take effect Thursday night as temperatures drop 10 degrees
item.description: Thursday morning temperatures are forecast to drop about 10 degrees Celsius from Wednesday, with parts of northeastern Gyeonggi Province and inland and mountainous Gangwon Province dipping below freezing. A cold wave advisory will take effect after midnight Thursday for most inland areas. It is issued from October to April when the morning low is forecast to fall at least 10 degrees from the previous day to 3 degrees or below and to run at least 3 degrees below normal. Morning lows on Thursday are forecast at 0 to 10 degrees nationwide. Frost will form in inland areas and ice in eastern Gyeonggi Province, inland and mountainous Gangwon Province, North Chungcheong Provice, northeastern North Jeolla Province and inland central and northeastern mountainous areas of North Gyeongsang Province. Daytime highs will stay between 14 and 19 degrees. Temperatures will swing by 15 degrees or more between morning and afternoon. item.title: Busan authorities guide shark out of canal on third attempt
item.description: Authorities in the southeastern port city of Busan successfully guided a shark out of a city canal Wednesday on their third attempt after the animal spent more than a month trapped there. The shark — named "Bukangi" after Bukhang, the Korean word for North Port — was first spotted in the canal Sept. 18. Since then, the canal park has turned into a major attraction, drawing over 1.6 million visitors as of Sunday. A joint rescue team involving municipal and Coast Guard officials used a net secured to a flat floating platform to drive the shark out of the canal at Busan's North Port, located about 330 kilometers southeast of Seoul. Authorities began the operation around 10 a.m., steering the shark toward Marina Bridge with the net. The shark, which had been swimming near the bridge, was spotted in waters outside the canal near a pier at around 6 p.m. The sighting indicated that Bukangi had left the canal, at least for the time being. item.title: [VIDEO] Beyond the cup: Korea's evolving cafe industry
item.description: Korea is home to roughly 100,000 cafes. How did the coffee industry thrive to this extent in a country that is not historically known for coffee? Looking at Mega MGC Coffee — the chain with the largest number of branches in Korea — two key factors emerge. On average, a Korean consumes nearly 400 cups of coffee per year, which is almost three times the global average. For Koreans, coffee is less of a leisurely break and more of a functional "potion" used to endure demanding workloads. Because of this, cafes in Korea generally adopt one of two distinct strategies: they either position themselves as high-end establishments, or they brand themselves as low-cost options to maximize profit through high sales volume rather than high margins per drink. Mega MGC Coffee falls into the latter category. By pricing an iced Americano at around 2,000 won($1.5) for a 710ml cup, the company focuses on becoming part of the daily routine for consumers rather than making a large profit from each sale. item.title: Top US envoy cites 'turbulence' in S. Korea-US alliance amid rift in security, trade priorities
item.description: The top U.S. envoy to South Korea on Wednesday described bilateral relations between Seoul and Washington as being in a state of "turbulence," stressing efforts to move the alliance forward into a stronger and more equal partnership. U.S. Ambassador Michelle Steel's remarks come amid apparent friction in the security and trade ties, from implementing their summit agreement from last October and intelligence sharing on North Korea to Seoul's push to retake wartime operational control (OPCON) from Washington. "This is, kind of, like a turbulence that we are going through between the Republic of Korea and the U.S.," she said during a dialogue session hosted by the American Chamber of Commerce in Korea (AMCHAM), referring to South Korea by its official name. "An alliance does not mean it stays always the same. It can be weaker, and we can move forward to be stronger. This is exactly what we are working on," she said. item.title: Lee Sun-bin embraces comedy, chaos in movie about college entrance exam
item.description: In the upcoming comedy film "Ugly Duckling Ms. Maeng," actor Lee Sun-bin plays Maeng Bo-ram, an earnest provincial high school teacher who unexpectedly finds herself locked away in a top-secret camp to draft questions for the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT). Ahead of the movie's theatrical release, Lee expressed both anxiety and anticipation during a recent interview in Seoul, saying the unique subject of the annual exam posed its own challenges. "This moment right before the release is both the time I want to avoid and the moment I look forward to," Lee told The Korea Times at a cafe in Seoul on Wednesday. "I tend to be harsh on myself and worry about my shortcomings. At the same time, I am deeply curious whether audiences will recognize actors’ intentions behind the performance. It feels like I am scared, but also eager to face the verdict as soon as possible." The movie centers on the 40-day isolation period where test developers are completely cut off from the outside world under strict security. item.title: K-pop soars on Asian tour revenue, physical album sales
item.description: K-pop is riding a surge in concert ticket and physical album sales, two of the industry's key revenue streams, as data released this month showed the genre dominating Asia's touring market and closing in on 100 million album sales for the year. The two businesses sit at the core of K-pop agencies' earnings. At HYBE, concerts brought in 647.7 billion won ($488.5 million) of its record 1.45 trillion won in second-quarter revenue, while albums and digital music accounted for 326.8 billion won, followed closely by merchandise and licensing at 310.6 billion won. K-pop acts took six of the 10 highest-grossing touring spots in Asia over the past year, led by boy band Seventeen, which grossed $97.4 million and sold 661,088 tickets, according to U.S. concert industry publication Pollstar's Asia Focus Top Touring Artists chart. The chart covers shows played between Aug. 1, 2025, and July 31, 2026. K-pop acts filled the chart's top four spots. TWICE came in second with $76.18 million, followed by TXT and BTS, which grossed $49.07 million in Asia as part of its "ARIRANG" world tour. BLACKPINK and EN

item.title: Prosecutors seek 5-year prison term for pastor over courthouse riot
item.description: Prosecutors on Wednesday requested a five-year prison term for conservative activist pastor Jeon Kwang-hoon over his alleged involvement in a courthouse riot last year by supporters of former President Yoon Suk Yeol. The Seoul Western District Prosecutors Office sought the sentence during a hearing at the Seoul Western District Court, where Jeon faced multiple charges, including instigating trespassing in special-protection buildings. Jeon is accused of being behind pro-Yoon protesters' violence at the same court on Jan. 19 last year, following the court's decision to extend Yoon's detention over his martial law declaration in December 2024. The prosecution also charged Jeon with violating the Assembly and Demonstration Act and obstructing general traffic for urging rally participants gathered in Gwanghwamun Square to march toward the court one day before the violence. item.title: IVE turns Seoul's futuristic DDP into K-pop comeback stage
item.description: Seoul is transforming one of its most iconic architectural landmarks into a high-octane venue for K-pop, partnering with girl group IVE to launch its latest comeback campaign at Dongdaemun Design Plaza (DDP) in an effort to turn global fandom into tourism revenues and longer hotel stays. The Seoul Metropolitan Government and Seoul Design Foundation are supporting the campaign, titled “DIVE IN TO LIGHT,” which began Monday at DDP and runs through Nov. 30. The building’s exterior displays special videos featuring IVE, with a more elaborate presentation planned to coincide with the release of the group’s new album on Monday, when synchronized laser effects and lighting will accompany its new music. A promotional booth is operating at DDP from 5:30 p.m. to 11 p.m. through Nov. 1, featuring album-themed photo zones and displays of hero masks worn by IVE members. item.title: Gwanghwamun memorial garden draws 500,000 visitors, celebrates Swedish ties
item.description: Seoul’s Garden of Gratitude has drawn more than 500,000 visitors in its first 160 days, as the memorial space prepares to celebrate its ties with Sweden through a weekend of cultural events, performances and a special light display. The Seoul Metropolitan Government said the garden recorded 500,157 visitors as of Monday, according to an automated counting system. Located at Gwanghwamun Square, the garden honors countries and veterans who fought in the 1950-53 Korean War and invites visitors to reflect on freedom, peace and international solidarity. Its outdoor installation, “23 Lights of Gratitude,” symbolizes appreciation for the countries that supported Korea during the war, while an underground exhibition hall called Freedom Hall uses digital media to tell the story of the conflict and Korea’s transformation from an aid recipient into a donor nation. Sweden has added a new element to the memorial, donating syenite quarried in Ekeröd, Sweden, in August, the city said. item.title: Seoul Wellness Travel Week brings meditation, food, art to city
item.description: Seoul will turn meditation, traditional cuisine and live music into a citywide invitation to slow down as it hosts Seoul Wellness Travel Week beginning Saturday, with programs centered on Gangnam District and eight wellness destinations across the city. Organized by the Seoul Metropolitan Government, the 12-day event, running until Nov. 4, will showcase experiences designed around three themes: rest, food and culture, under the slogan “Seoul, Defines the Next Wellness.” At Bongeunsa Temple, visitors can join sound-bowl meditation, yoga, tea gatherings and restorative exercise on Saturday and Sunday, with 15 wellness programs planned across the two days. Highlights include a meditation session led by Ven. Geumgang, chair of the Jogye Order’s Seon Meditation Committee, and an evening walking meditation through the temple grounds. Most temple programs cost 5,000 won ($3.60), while Ven. Geumgang’s meditation session is free. item.title: Trump and Republicans blame France's immigrants for riots without evidence
item.description: PARIS — U.S. President Donald Trump and leading Republicans are trying to leverage widespread riots in France ahead of midterm congressional elections by making unsubstantiated claims that the social unrest in Europe is caused by Muslim migrants. Peaceful nationwide demonstrations in France over the high cost of living and in support of students' grievances over underfunded schools turned violent over the weekend, with masked rioters committing vandalism and clashing with overwhelmed police. In Italy’s finance and fashion capital of Milan on Saturday, rioters clashed with police, looted stores and set property on fire. Here's a closer look at the facts. CLAIM: Migrants of Muslim heritage are doing most of the damage in France and Italy. THE FACTS: It is difficult to know the exact sociological makeup of the protesters, but no one group has been singled out as being responsible for the violence. item.title: Korean won extends gains against US dollar on strong exports
item.description: The Korean won extended its gains to hit a fresh two-year high against the U.S. dollar Wednesday, supported by strong exports and foreign inflows. The won was quoted at 1,325.2 won per dollar at 3:30 p.m., up 2.9 won from the close of the previous stock trading session. For a fourth straight session, the won marked the highest level since Oct. 2, 2024. Earlier in the day, government data showed that the nation's exports more than doubled to US$61.6 billion in the first 20 days of October, driven by robust shipments of semiconductor. Foreign purchased a net 659.9 billion won ($497.3 million) worth of local shares during the latest regular stock trading session, with the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index gaining 3.29 percent to close at 5,735.66.

item.description: The Korean Peninsula faces a rapidly evolving threat environment, U.S. Forces Korea (USFK) Commander Gen. Xavier Brunson and a senior U.S. official said in back-to-back warnings from Seoul and Washington, raising questions about how those changes could affect the timing of the transfer of wartime operational control (OPCON). Their remarks followed a renewed dispute over the OPCON transfer after Brunson suggested on Oct. 14 that evolving threats called for new transition standards, drawing objections from Seoul’s defense ministry and an unusual response from President Lee Jae Myung. “Our security environment is not standing still. item.title: Lee says AI should be used to bridge health care gaps worldwide
item.description: President Lee Jae Myung said Wednesday that artificial intelligence (AI) technology should be used responsibly in the health care sector to bridge health care gaps worldwide. The president delivered the message in a speech to the World Bio Summit 2026 in Seoul, which was read on his behalf by his senior secretary for social affairs, Kim Kyoung-ja. The World Health Organization is hosting the event Wednesday and Thursday in collaboration with the Korean government. "In the health care sector, which is directly connected to human lives, AI technology should be used safely and responsibly to bridge gaps in medical services worldwide," the president said. The summit adopted the "AI Healthcare Seoul Declaration," calling for global solidarity to ensure that the benefits from AI innovations are shared by all and that AI technology is used in safe and responsible manners. "Narrowing gaps between countries in the health care sector and ensuring that everyone has access to proper medical services is the task of our time, and everyone should work together to accomplish it," Lee noted.

item.title: Seoul eyes long-term digital infrastructure projects via sovereign wealth fund
item.description: SEJONG — Korea plans to provide patient capital for long-term digital infrastructure projects through the country's planned sovereign wealth fund, the second vice finance minister has said. Second Vice Finance Minister Huh Chang outlined the plan during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Finance Ministers' Meeting held in Hong Kong from Tuesday to Wednesday, according to the Ministry of Finance and Economy. Huh's remarks came after Korea unveiled plans earlier this year to launch a new sovereign wealth fund in 2027 to make continuous investments in cutting-edge and strategic industries. During one of the sessions at the finance ministerial meeting, Huh highlighted the importance of public funding and the mobilization of private capital in pursuing major projects in future growth industries. The senior policymaker said that the country plans to provide long-term patient capital, which refers to investment that does not require immediate returns, for digital infrastructure projects through the sovereign wealth fund. item.title: Mercedes-Benz Korea promotes safer driving with Beyond Driving campaign
item.description: Mercedes-Benz Korea is expanding its road safety efforts, drawing on its automotive expertise and safety experience to promote more considerate driving. The company’s Corporate Social Responsibility Committee recently launched Beyond Driving, a campaign that encourages motorists to adopt safer everyday driving habits, extending its safety initiatives beyond children to drivers of all ages. The committee has promoted road safety in Korea for over a decade, starting with MobileKids, a traffic safety education program for children in 2014. Its initiatives have since expanded to include school-zone safety campaigns, online and in-person education programs and radio campaigns, collectively reaching more than 50,000 children. This year, the committee broadened its focus to drivers nationwide with Beyond Driving, emphasizing that safer roads depend not only on compliance with traffic laws but also on drivers being considerate of one another and yielding when necessary. item.title: NK leader's sister, military marshal inspect border fortification site, warn of 'overwhelming' responses
item.description: Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, and a military marshal have inspected fortification work along the inter-Korean border, with Pyongyang warning of an "overwhelming" military response to what it called enemy provocations, state media reported Wednesday. The inspection came after the South Korean military vowed Tuesday to take "decisive" action if the North stages further provocations, following Pyongyang's threat to deploy strike means along the border. Pak Jong-chon, an adviser to the North's Ministry of National Defense, inspected key positions along the southern border the previous day to review progress on a project to fortify the border, according to the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA). During the inspection, Pak accused the enemy of making "deliberate, premeditated and absurd" claims that North Korean troops had crossed the border. "Our army knows where our borderline is better than any others, and we are doing what we should do in our territory," he was quoted as saying. item.title: Samsung Biologics Q3 net income down over 20%
item.description: Samsung Biologics, the biotech arm of Samsung Group, on Wednesday reported its third-quarter net profit of 391.1 billion won ($295.2 million), down 21.2 percent from a year earlier. The contract development and manufacturing organization (CDMO) service provider, which offers comprehensive development and manufacturing solutions, said in a regulatory filing that it posted 640.1 billion won in operating profit for the quarter, compared with 633.5 billion won a year ago. Revenue rose 18.5 percent to 1.49 trillion won. The company attributed its sales increase to full-scale operations at four plants in Songdo, just west of Seoul, a ramp-up in production at its fifth plant, as well as sales generated from its first U.S.-based biomanufacturing facility in Rockville, Maryland, acquired in March. The company said it will continue to expand its contract development and manufacturing (CDMO) business, with cumulative contract orders for this year reaching $22 billion. item.title: Actor Eum Moon-suk to marry girlfriend in January
item.description: Actor Eum Moon-suk is set to get married in January. A representative of his agency, Ghost Studio, told Hankook Ilbo on Wednesday that Eum “will marry his girlfriend in January next year.” According to reports, his fiancée currently works as a model, and the couple will tie the knot after dating for a long time. Born in 1982, Eum made his debut as a singer in 2005 and appeared on Mnet’s dance competition program “Dancing 9” in 2013. He later transitioned to acting, taking on a wide range of roles in television dramas, including “The Fiery Priest,” “Tell Me What You Saw,” “Backstreet Rookie,” “Hello, Me!,” “Good Job,” “Let's Go to the Moon” and “City of Shadows,” as well as films such as “Pipeline,” “The Roundup 2,” “6/45” and “My Name Is Loh Kiwan.” Eum drew particular attention for his role as Yang-bae in director Na Hong-jin’s latest film, “Hope,” which was released in July. item.title: Gangnam arson attack renews alarm over elderly men with grudges
item.description: A man in his 70s arrested on suspicion of injuring 19 people in an arson attack cited a personal grudge as his motive, renewing concern over elderly people driven by resentment starting fires. On Tuesday, two buildings in Seoul’s Gangnam District were set on fire and the suspect was caught fleeing. He mostly acknowledged planning and committing the arson, police said Wednesday. He is believed to have harbored a grievance against patent law firms over their handling of a trademark registration. When reporters asked about his motive, he shouted that the firms had cheated him. Asked what he would say to the victims, he replied, “Tell them to stop cheating people.” The suspect had already been detained in 2022 for preparing to commit arson after visiting the same two law firms, dousing employees with gasoline and threatening them with a lighter. The case is the latest in a pattern of arson attacks by older adults acting on accumulated grudges. One of the most striking was the 2008 arson of Sungnyemun — Korea's National Treasure No. 1, built in 1398 as the main southern gate of Seoul'

item.title: Korea's crypto tax faces 4th delay as gov't turns cautious amid low approval ratings
item.description: Korea’s tax on cryptocurrency gains, scheduled to take effect in January, could face a fourth postponement as the government turns cautious amid mounting calls for a delay from investors, the industry and lawmakers from both ruling and opposition parties. Authorities have defended the levy on the principle that income should be taxed and on grounds of fairness across asset classes. However, the government’s recent pledge to reassess tax infrastructure and market conditions has fueled expectations of another postponement. The subtle shift comes as falling stock prices and tighter property taxation have already frustrated investors, raising concerns that crypto taxation could provoke further backlash. Low approval ratings for President Lee Jae Myung and the ruling party are adding to the political pressure. The issue is particularly sensitive among young investors. Under the current timetable, the first filing and payment deadline would fall in May 2028, immediately after parliamentary elections that April. On Wednesday, Rep. item.title: Election official found dead after special counsel questioning
item.description: A National Election Commission (NEC) official was found dead Wednesday, a day after being questioned by a special counsel team investigating the election watchdog in connection with the unprecedented ballot shortages in the local elections. According to the sources, the official in his 40s was found in the flowerbed of an apartment building in Hwaseong, about 45 kilometers south of Seoul, at 7:06 a.m. with a suicide note expressing grievances he felt during the questioning. Police suspect he jumped from his apartment. The investigation team has been looking into why the ballot shortages happened and if any corruption or irregularities were involved in contracts for election-related supplies, such as early voting ballot boxes and voting site banners used in last year's presidential election and the June 3 local elections. The deceased underwent questioning at the investigation team's office Tuesday as a suspect over alleged obstruction of the bidding process and breach of trust. item.title: KB Life CEO joins campaign against illegal lending
item.description: KB Life Insurance CEO Jeong Mun-cheol has joined a nationwide campaign against illegal private lending, pledging to help protect the financially vulnerable and promote financial inclusion, the insurer said Wednesday. Launched in July by the Korea Inclusive Finance Agency, the “Finance That Saves Lives” campaign brings together financial institutions, government agencies and local governments. It follows a relay format, where participants share a message raising public awareness of inclusive finance and nominate the next person to carry it forward. The initiative aligns with the Lee Jae Myung administration’s push for inclusive finance, which includes expanding access to financial services, easing the burden on delinquent borrowers and cracking down on illegal lending. Jeong was nominated by KB Kookmin Bank CEO Lee Hwan-ju on Sept. 28. item.title: Appeals court slashes ex-justice minister's sentence to 9 years over martial law role
item.description: An appellate court on Wednesday significantly reduced former Justice Minister Park Sung-jae's sentence from 25 years to nine years in prison over his role in former President Yoon Suk Yeol's failed martial law bid. The Seoul High Court handed down the lighter sentence, convicting Park of playing a key role in an insurrection under Yoon's short-lived declaration of martial law in December 2024, while overturning a lower court's conviction on multiple other charges. The appellate court ruled Park was aware that Yoon's emergency decree did not meet the substantive and procedural conditions for martial law, and the declaration was made for unconstitutional and illegal purposes. It found Park's order for the chief of the immigration office at the justice ministry to have his official in charge of placing exit bans report to work constituted playing a key role in an insurrection, as well as his instruction to the head of correctional services to check the capacity of correctional facilities. item.title: Court sentences 3 ex-officials to suspended prison terms over 2019 deportation of N. Koreans
item.description: An appellate court on Wednesday handed down suspended prison terms for three former officials for forcibly repatriating two North Korean fishermen in 2019 despite their intention to defect to South Korea. The Seoul High Court upheld a lower court's guilty verdicts for Chung Eui-yong, former national security adviser; former National Intelligence Service Director Suh Hoon; and former Unification Minister Kim Yeon-chul. It, however, acquitted former Presidential chief of staff Noh Young-min, who had earlier been convicted over his involvement in the case. All four served in former President Moon Jae-in's administration in November 2019, when Seoul deported two North Korean fishermen back to North Korea after they were captured near the eastern maritime border. The fishermen had been accused of killing 16 crew members. The move sparked outcry from critics as the fishermen had expressed their intent to defect to South Korea, which maintains a policy of accepting North Korean defectors. item.title: Budget minister vows to review vulnerabilities in funding for firefighters
item.description: SEJONG — Korea's budget minister on Wednesday vowed to look into potential vulnerabilities in the country's funding for firefighters, amid concerns that they have become a financial burden for regional governments. "I agree that the issue needs to be carefully examined," Budget Minister Park Hong-geun said during a meeting with reporters in the central city of Sejong. "We have not yet held detailed internal discussions on how the situation should be improved," Park said. "We need to look into the issue with the presidential office, the interior ministry, the fire agency and regional governments." His remarks came after Gyeonggi Province Gov. Choo Mi-ae recently described firefighters as a "fiscal drain," triggering public backlash while drawing attention to underlying issues in the funding system. Choo's remarks were based on concerns that firefighting services have become a burden on local government finances, despite firefighters being classified as central government employees since 2020. item.title: Align Partners reveals 1.5% stake in SK Inc., sees 75% valuation discount
item.description: Align Partners disclosed that it holds a 1.5 percent stake in SK Inc. through its fund, arguing that the holding company's share price does not fully reflect the value of its key subsidiary, SK hynix. According to materials presented by Align CEO Lee Chang-hwan at the "13D Monitor Active-Passive Investor Summit" in New York on Tuesday (local time), the activist fund held 1,088,753 shares of SK Inc., representing 1.5 percent of the holding company's total outstanding shares. Lee described SK Inc. as an opportunity to gain exposure to world-class artificial intelligence assets at a discounted valuation. SK Inc. holds a 32.2 percent stake in SK Square, which in turn owns about 20 percent of SK hynix. It gives SK Inc. an effective stake of roughly 6.5 percent in the chipmaker. He explained that the value of SK Inc.'s indirect stake in SK hynix is subject to two layers of discounts due to its ownership structure. item.title: DPK considering parliamentary probe into Supreme Court chief amid impeachment calls
item.description: The ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK) said Wednesday it is considering launching a parliamentary investigation into Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae amid an ongoing debate within the party over whether to seek his impeachment. Following a meeting of the party's supreme council, DPK spokesperson Cho Gye-won told reporters that the party was considering launching such a probe to look into "specific grounds" for impeaching the chief justice after the ongoing parliamentary audit ends later this month. When asked whether the probe would be aimed at impeaching the chief justice, the lawmaker replied, "It is intended to shed light on the grounds for impeachment ... so it could be seen that way." The announcement came after DPK leader Kim Min-seok said on Friday that the party has begun discussing various options to impeach Cho. item.title: [COVER STORY] French residents of Korea blame unresponsive gov't for unrest
item.description: The public anger in France spilling over into unrest has been brewing for a long time, with little response from the government over calls for reforms for better education and living conditions, French nationals living in Korea say. They generally agree that the French government's long-standing neglect and inaction have fueled mounting public anger, saying people's concerns have long gone unheard. "Government hasn’t listened enough to people’s concerns about the climate, the economy and now education. When people repeatedly feel unheard, frustration builds up," Hugo Adam, a graduate student at Seoul National University, told The Korea Times. A French filmmaker, who spoke on condition of anonymity, agreed that the French government has failed to "listen to its people," despite the many protests that have taken place over the years. He said his family and friends back home are participating in the protests. The protests began in mid-September by students calling for a better education environment, including more teachers and improved school facilities. Illustrator Zoe Constans said it

item.title: Seoul stocks rebound over 3% on eased AI spending woes
item.description: Korean stocks rebounded Wednesday, recovering from the previous session's steep losses as semiconductor shares rallied on easing concerns over artificial intelligence (AI) spending. The Korean won strengthened against the U.S. dollar. The benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) gained 182.92 points, or 3.29 percent, to close at 5,735.66 after rising as high as 5,816.43. The sharp rally prompted the Korea Exchange (KRX) to activate a buy-side sidecar shortly before 11 a.m., temporarily suspending program buying for five minutes after KOSPI 200 futures rose more than 5 percent. It marked the first such activation in two months. The rebound came after the main index plunged nearly 4 percent the previous session amid renewed concerns over massive AI infrastructure spending. Investor sentiment improved after better-than-expected earnings from U.S. AI server maker Super Micro Computer helped ease worries over AI-related investments, lifting shares of chip giants Samsung Electronics and SK hynix. item.title: Incheon locals oppose plan to move Overseas Koreans Agency to Sejong
item.description: Political parties, local officials and civic activists in Incheon are pushing back against the government’s plan to relocate the Overseas Koreans Agency (OKA) to Sejong, calling the decision unilateral and demanding it be scrapped. The Ministry of the Interior and Safety announced Oct. 13 that 44 ministries and agencies would relocate in phases beginning next year through 2031 as part of a national strategy to break up the capital area-centered administrative system. The agency, which oversees diaspora policy under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, is among the first six agencies slated to move — scheduled to leave its Incheon headquarters for the administrative city of Sejong by the first half of 2027. The OKA was originally established in Incheon following fierce competition among local governments, with the city selected for its proximity to Incheon International Airport and its symbolic significance as a gateway for the Korean diaspora. item.title: Korean doctor operates remotely from Seoul on pig in Shanghai
item.description: Sitting at a console in Seoul, a Korean doctor successfully operated on a pig using a surgical robot about 870 kilometers away in Shanghai, marking Korea’s first cross-border telesurgery demonstration using a commercial platform. Kang Seok-ho, a professor of urology at Korea University College of Medicine, says the technology could profoundly transform surgical care, allowing doctors to operate from distant facilities and across borders, including on patients in disaster zones and battlefields. “I was delighted. I also found it remarkable that I could actually perform surgery in Shanghai from here,” Kang said in a recent interview with The Korea Times. The demonstration was conducted on Friday at Coex in Seoul during the Korean Urological Association’s annual meeting. The Toumai system developed by China’s MicroPort MedBot was used, according to the hospital. Telesurgery allows a physician to control surgical instruments through a communications network rather than being physically present in the same surgery as the patient. Unlike remote consultations, it involves the surgeon

item.title: Is AI investment slowing Naver's profits?
item.description: The outlook for internet giant Naver’s third-quarter earnings is turning gloomy, with analysts expecting operating profit to decline by double digits, citing spending on artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure and the slow monetization of AI services. According to market tracker FnGuide, the brokerage consensus estimate for Naver's third-quarter operating profit stood at 500 billion won ($377.5 million), down 12.4 percent from 570.66 billion won a year earlier, as of Wednesday. This contrasts with the projected 12 percent increase in revenue to 3.51 trillion won from 3.14 trillion won over the same period. Among the various factors, rising costs appear to be the biggest contributor to the decline. These include increased marketing expenses for Naver's commerce business, World Cup broadcasting rights costs reflected in the third-quarter results and higher depreciation expenses stemming from investments in graphics processing units (GPUs). item.title: Why has video of former presidential couple singing together surfaced now?
item.description: A video of former President Yoon Suk Yeol and his wife, Kim Keon Hee, singing a duet has been released, featuring the couple at the center of Korea’s first-ever case of a former president and first lady being detained simultaneously. The video was posted on social media by a close aide to Kim, prompting speculation that it may be intended to build public support for her release ahead of the expiration of her detention period at the end of this month. The video was posted Saturday by Jung Ji-won, a former administrative official at the presidential office who served as Kim’s aide during the Yoon administration. It shows the couple, dressed casually, singing “All I Ask of You” from the musical “The Phantom of the Opera” at what appears to be their residence. In the musical, the characters Christine and Raoul sing the song as they pledge their eternal love to each other. “Another hobby of the first lady is giving singing lessons to the president,” Jung wrote. “They were such an affectionate couple that they even practiced songs as duets.” Jung’s account was created in

item.title: Capital soundness looms over major insurers' CEO reappointment decisions
item.description: With the terms of major insurers’ CEOs set to expire early next year, the companies’ capital strength is emerging as a key factor in their chances of reappointment, particularly as new rules requiring insurers to hold stronger financial cushion against losses are set to take effect in 2027, industry officials said Wednesday. The terms of Samsung Life Insurance CEO Hong Won-hak, Samsung Fire & Marine Insurance CEO Lee Mun-hwa, DB Insurance CEO Jeong Jong-pyo and Kyobo Life Insurance co-CEO Cho Dae-kyu are all due to expire in March. All four companies reported higher consolidated net profit in the first half of this year. Samsung Life posted 1.97 trillion won, followed by Samsung Fire & Marine with 1.37 trillion won, DB Insurance with 979.6 billion won and Kyobo Life with 704.8 billion won. item.title: Solidigm's potential Nasdaq IPO: Can Korean regulators intervene?
item.description: Korean regulators are facing calls to block a potential Nasdaq listing of Solidigm, SK hynix's U.S.-based NAND flash memory subsidiary, amid concerns that the move could undermine protections for shareholders of its Korean parent company, industry officials said Wednesday. "President Lee Jae Myung should use every means at his disposal to stop the listing," said Rep. Ahn Cheol-soo of the main opposition People Power Party. "If Solidigm goes public, its rising valuation and shareholder base could dilute SK hynix shareholders' indirect stake in the company." Solidigm is owned by AI Company, a U.S.-based entity controlled by SK hynix. Further up the ownership chain are SK Square and SK Group's holding company, SK Inc. The dispute underscores Korea's complex corporate ownership structures, long criticized by retail investors as a factor behind the "Korea discount." In July, Korea introduced rules to protect minority shareholders from unfavorable dual listings. Under the rules, companies seeking to list carved-out subsidiaries domestically must meet shareholder approval and protection require

item.title: Hyundai Mobis to test viability of local auto chips
item.description: Hyundai Mobis will focus on verifying the real-world applicability and commercial viability of locally developed automotive semiconductors this year, as the industry seeks to reduce reliance on overseas suppliers amid the shift toward software-defined vehicles (SDVs), the auto parts maker said Wednesday. The company identified 19 joint system semiconductor projects with Korean companies over the past year, with development underway on 13 chips. Nine of the 13 have designated target vehicle models, bringing the projects closer to real-world application. Hyundai Mobis unveiled the progress at its second Auto Semicon Korea forum in Seongnam, Gyeonggi Province. Participation expanded to 53 companies and institutions this year, up from 27 last year, as collaboration widened to include software, chip design intellectual property, packaging, testing and functional safety. The forum was launched last year to strengthen Korea’s automotive semiconductor supply chain by connecting automakers, parts suppliers, chip designers, foundries and research institutions. item.title: Apple to make Siri AI available in Korea this month: sources
item.description: Korean customers will be able to use Apple's generative artificial intelligence (AI)-powered assistant soon, as the tech giant is set to support Korean on its Siri AI starting this month, industry sources said Wednesday. The latest service expansion comes after Apple made a beta launch of the new Siri in English in September. Siri AI is a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding, broad world knowledge, onscreen awareness and even more systemwide app actions, the company said in a release. Another function of Siri AI is its visual intelligence, which offers powerful image understanding and multimodal capabilities. item.title: Almonty Korea donates $9,000 to rural high school in Gangwon Province
item.description: Almonty Korea Tungsten, which operates a tungsten mine in Gangwon Province, said Wednesday it has donated 12 million won ($9,000) to Sangdong High School, a small rural school that turned to baseball as a way to avoid closing. The company handed over the donation Tuesday at the school in Sangdong, a town in Yeongwol County. It is the fourth consecutive year the company has supported the school’s baseball team. The Korean company is a subsidiary of Almonty Industries, a tungsten producer listed on the Nasdaq. Its Sangdong mine, located in the same town, began active mining in December last year. Tungsten is a hard, heat-resistant metal used in industries from electronics to defense. Sangdong High School faced closure when its enrollment fell to just three students. In 2023, with help from the local community, it reinvented itself as a school specializing in baseball. The team has since made quick progress. item.title: Korea space agency joins int'l satellite alliance for global disaster relief
item.description: The Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA) said Wednesday it has joined the board of the International Charter: Space and Major Disasters, a global partnership in which space agencies provide satellite images to countries hit by disasters. KASA joined during the charter’s 56th regular board meeting at Ochanomizu Sola City in Tokyo, which opened Monday and continues through Friday. The space agency will take part in setting the charter’s policies as a board member starting in 2027. The charter is a voluntary, nonbinding partnership set up by space agencies for humanitarian, nonprofit purposes. When a major disaster such as an earthquake, typhoon or heavy snowfall strikes, member agencies take images of the affected area with their satellites, provide them to the country hit by the disaster and help analyze the damage. It has 17 member agencies from countries including the United States, France, Japan, China and India, as well as the European Space Agency. The board, its main decision-making body, reviews and approves major policies and sets plans and strategies. It holds regular meeti

item.title: High tech, universal access propel Seoul subway to top of global rankings
item.description: When international travelers step onto a Seoul subway train platform, they are often struck by the lack of trash on the floor, delayed trains or dead zones on their smartphones. That seamless efficiency has now earned the Korean capital top honors in two major international transit rankings. British lifestyle media outlet "Time Out" placed the Korean capital fifth in its 2026 global transit survey — up three spots from last year — with 91.1 percent of surveyed residents expressing satisfaction. Meanwhile, CNN featured Seoul in its roundup of the world's 18 best metro systems, highlighting its cleanliness, high safety standards and tech-forward amenities. Behind the global accolades lies decades of aggressive infrastructure investment, particularly in passenger safety, accessibility and digital convenience. item.title: USFK commander calls for more frequent combined drills with S. Korea throughout year
item.description: The top U.S. military commander in South Korea called Wednesday for conducting more spread-out combined exercises between the allies throughout the year, rather than relying on the current biannual drills, citing the need to better adapt to an evolving security environment. U.S. Forces Korea (USFK) Commander Gen. Xavier Brunson made the remarks during a dialogue session in Seoul, saying he met with the South's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) Chairman Gen. Jin Yong-sung earlier this week to discuss their next springtime drills. item.title: Shoppers turn to warehouse stores as grocery bills climb
item.description: For Kim Eun-young, a 42-year-old mother of two living in Seoul’s Gwangjin District, a monthly trip to Costco has become routine this year. She used to pick up what she needed at a nearby supermarket, but rising prices prompted her to change her shopping habits. She said buying groceries and household essentials in bulk seems more economical, at least for her family of four. “The bill is bigger each time, but buying in bulk works out cheaper for the same amount,” Kim said. “I mainly buy food we eat regularly and everyday household essentials, and divide the food into meal-sized portions for storage.” Kim’s changing habits reflect a growing appetite for warehouse shopping as consumers seek relief from high prices. According to market tracker WiseApp Retail, combined estimated card spending at Costco and Emart Traders totaled a record 1.45 trillion won ($1.09 billion) in September. The estimates are based on a sample of Korean consumers’ credit and debit card payments. They exclude cash and bank transfers and therefore differ from the retailers’ reported revenue. Warehouse ret

item.title: Hanwha-Anthropic exhibition explores AI, human values through art
item.description: An exhibition exploring questions of how artificial intelligence (AI) systems work and how they are aligned with human values will take place in Seoul beginning this week, organizers said Wednesday. Titled "AS_____AS POSSIBLE," the exhibition co-hosted by the Hanwha Foundation of Culture and U.S. firm Anthropic, builder of the AI platform Claude, will open at the Centre Pompidou Hanwha on Friday, according to the organizers. The exhibition features five Korean artists and teams — MinOhrichar, Inhwa Yeom, Ubac Studio, Kahee Jeong and Mirim Chu -- who used Claude for their commissioned works on display. The title of the exhibition comes from questions surrounding the purpose and realm of technologies, with the possibility of the blank in the title being filled with words such as accurate, understandable and aligned. The exhibition runs through Nov. 13.

item.title: Seoul Architecture Festival draws 40,000 visitors in extended monthlong run
item.description: The 18th Seoul Architecture Festival drew about 40,000 citizens and architects during its run, which was extended to about a month this year, the Seoul Metropolitan Government said Wednesday. The festival was held from Sept. 15 to Oct. 11 at the Seoul Hall of Urbanism & Architecture in central Seoul under the theme “Assembling Seoul: Discovering Seoul.” Last year’s two-week edition drew 19,505 visitors. Its centerpiece exhibition, created in collaboration with a photographer, placed photos of Seoul’s urban architecture throughout a maze-like space so that visitors could look at familiar city scenes in a new way. The festival’s director built the exhibition spaces from recycled wooden pallets to keep down costs and environmental impact. An exhibition of the 10 winners of the 44th Seoul Architecture Awards, the city’s annual prize for buildings, was led by the grand prize winner, the Seo-Seoul Museum of Art, designed by THE_SYSTEM LAB. item.title: US ambassador urges fair treatment for American firms in Korea
item.description: U.S. Ambassador to Korea Michelle Steel on Wednesday called on Seoul to ensure that American companies operating in Korea can compete on a level playing field, amid U.S. concerns over regulations affecting firms such as Coupang. "American companies in Korea deserve to compete on a level playing field, fairly and without discrimination," Steel said in her opening remarks at a special luncheon hosted by the American Chamber of Commerce in Korea (AMCHAM) in Seoul. The event also featured Gen. Xavier Brunson, commander of U.S. Forces Korea (USFK). Coupang, a U.S.-listed e-commerce firm that is active primarily in Korea, disclosed a data breach affecting over 33.6 million customers late last year, leading to an investigation and sanctions. In response, 50 U.S. Republican politicians signed a letter accusing Seoul of “targeted and discriminatory actions” against American companies, citing the Coupang case. Seoul has rejected the claims of discriminatory treatment, insisting that the investigation has been carried out in accordance with domestic law. The ambassador, addressing concerns ove

item.title: Songdo opens biomanufacturing training center for global workforce
item.description: A new biomanufacturing training facility opened in Songdo, Incheon, on Monday to train workers from low and middle-income countries in vaccine and biopharmaceutical production. Incheon Free Economic Zone (IFEZ) authorities said the Global Bio Campus training facility held an opening ceremony at Yonsei University’s International Campus in Incheon, attended by World Health Organization (WHO) Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Health Minister Jeong Eun-kyeong and IFEZ Commissioner Kim Jong-cheol. The facility was established in Songdo as part of efforts launched after WHO designated Korea as a Global Training Hub for Biomanufacturing (GTH-B) in February 2022. The ceremony also reviewed progress on the global biomanufacturing workforce training initiative and the development of its training infrastructure. item.title: Digital technology brings Korea's architectural heritage to life
item.description: Korea’s ancient architecture is moving beyond the ruins, with digital technology offering new ways to preserve historic sites and bring them to life for modern audiences. The National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage will host an international symposium on digital documentation and use of architectural heritage Nov. 4 at the WesternLife Hotel in Iksan, North Jeolla Province. The event will examine how digital records of historic buildings can support preservation, reconstruction and public engagement, drawing on examples from Korea, France and China. The symposium will also explore how cultural heritage data is being used beyond academic research, including in video games and immersive media, as researchers seek new ways to connect audiences with historic sites. The program features a keynote address by Kang Hyun of the institute on preserving and using architectural heritage through digital technology, followed by five presentations. Min Hwang-sik, also of the institute, will discuss findings and challenges from digital reconstruction research at Mireuksa, an ancient temple site

item.title: Rarely opened gate links 2 Seoul palaces for exclusive night tours
item.description: Visitors will be able to walk between Changdeok Palace and Changgyeong Palace in central Seoul at night next month through a gate that is normally closed to the public, as part of a ticketed night tour, the Korea Heritage Service said Wednesday. The tour, called “Donggwol Dongnak,” runs from Nov. 10-15. It is organized by the agency’s Royal Palaces and Tombs Center and the Korea Heritage Agency. The two palaces were together known as Donggwol, or the “Eastern Palaces,” during the Joseon Dynasty (1392-1910) because they stood east of Gyeongbok Palace, the main royal palace. The 110-minute program combines a guided tour of both palaces with free time to explore their rear gardens. Guides playing court painters from Dohwaseo, the Joseon-era royal bureau of painting, will lead participants through major halls of Changgyeong Palace and the rear garden of Changdeok Palace. Short plays about historical figures linked to each site will be staged at four stops along the route. item.title: Coastal coffee capital of Korea mixes beachside reading with 'text hip' trend
item.description: Korea's tourism authorities are combining two of the country's biggest cultural obsessions — coffee and reading — for a seaside getaway this week on the nation's eastern coast. The Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and the Korea Tourism Organization (KTO) are hosting "Sea 24 Hours: Book Trip," a five-day outdoor reading event at Anmok Beach in Gangneung, running through Sunday. The event taps into "text hip," a viral trend among young Koreans who view reading physical books as a stylish, aesthetic lifestyle statement rather than just a quiet hobby. It is paired with the annual Gangneung Coffee Festival, which draws roughly 300,000 visitors to a coastal city widely celebrated as Korea’s specialty coffee capital. Set against a pine grove stretching along the sandy shoreline, the initiative also aims to encourage travelers to slow down, encouraging festivalgoers to linger longer in the region through a relaxed blend of coastal views, local coffee, and literature. The book lounge, open daily from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m., offers about 200 books in four themed sections: food, photography

item.title: Japanese tourists flock to Haman County for unique cultural experiences
item.description: “Metcha kirei!” The Japanese exclamation, which means "it's really beautiful," rang out at Mujinjeong Pavilion in Haman County, South Gyeongsang Province, as dusk settled on the evening of Oct. 15. When local residents set fire to around 3,000 nak-hwa sticks — made by wrapping oak charcoal powder in hanji, traditional Korean paper, and twisting it into long wicks — a torrent of vivid red sparks rained down over the pond. Reflected on the water, the sparks blurred the boundary between heaven and earth, creating a dreamlike atmosphere. Each time the suspended lines were shaken, cascades of sparks poured down. “I’ve never seen fireworks that fall downward rather than shoot up into the sky. They’re truly magical,” said Sato Mio, 44, who visited from Osaka, Japan. “I’m amazed by the ingenuity of Koreans in the past, who created such beautiful displays of fire.” Her travel companion, Suzuki Ren, 47, gave a thumbs-up. “I’ve visited Seoul and Busan many times, but this is my first time in Haman,” he said. “I’d definitely like to come back if I get the chance.” Th

item.title: Korean Air tests UAM operations on island routes off Incheon
item.description: Korean Air said Wednesday it has successfully tested urban air mobility (UAM) operations on island routes off Korea's west coast, marking a step toward expanding the technology beyond population centers. The carrier conducted the demonstration Tuesday using a surrogate aircraft in cooperation with KT Corp., Hyundai Motor and Hyundai Engineering & Construction near the western port city of Incheon. Korean Air used its in-house Air Control & Routing Orchestrated Skyway System (ACROSS) to manage flight operations and air traffic, testing the system's capabilities in an island environment. The airline plans to complete the first phase of Incheon's UAM control system project in December as part of its efforts to develop traffic management and flight operations systems for future air taxi services.

item.title: District in Seoul automates bulky waste disposal with one-shot AI app
item.description: A district in Seoul is turning to computer vision to overhaul one of the most tedious chores of urban living: getting rid of old furniture and discarded household appliances. Eunpyeong District in northwestern Seoul has launched a pilot program using an artificial intelligence (AI) mobile application that allows residents to arrange bulky waste disposal by snapping a single photograph. The service is the first of its kind to be deployed by a municipality in Korea. Around the world, forward-looking metropolitan centers are racing to integrate machine learning into municipal waste management. Cities like Singapore and Zurich have deployed AI-powered robotic sorters and smart sensors in public bins to optimize collection. However, automating the resident-facing reporting process through consumer computer vision remains a rare frontier in smart city innovation — placing the Seoul district at the forefront of AI-driven urban convenience. In Korea, disposing of large items requires reporting each piece to the local district office and paying a designated collection fee. Previously, Eunpyeon

item.title: TWICE's Jihyo leaves JYP after 21 years to launch own agency
item.description: Jihyo, a member of K-pop girl group TWICE, said Wednesday she has left JYP Entertainment to establish her own agency. In a handwritten letter posted on social media, Jihyo said she had ended her contract with JYP, where she had been for 21 years since childhood. "I have established Emithaus," she wrote. "Through this new home, I hope to freely explore even the possibilities within myself that I have yet to discover." The 29-year-old singer added, "I will approach every future choice and activity with greater care and a stronger sense of responsibility, as I step out of a familiar environment and continue my work in a new way." Jihyo plans to pursue her solo music career under the new agency while continuing activities with TWICE. JYP Entertainment, one of Korea's major K-pop agencies, had managed Jihyo since she joined the company as a trainee before TWICE's 2015 debut.

item.title: US envoy Witkoff to meet Putin; Trump presses Kyiv to settle
item.description: OSLO/KYIV/WASHINGTON — U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday after what a U.S. official called "constructive" talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway, as President Donald Trump said it was time for Ukraine to end the war. The U.S. official said Ukraine brought forward new ideas and proposals to the Oslo talks, which also involved the leaders of Norway and Finland and European and NATO representatives, and that participants made "meaningful progress" toward a coordinated approach to engaging Russia. The official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the talks covered "key elements of a comprehensive peace framework," including security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic plan and a broader European security architecture. Witkoff would aim to "create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations," the official said. item.title: Korean heritage schools in Japan turn to parents for curriculum overhaul
item.description: When heritage language schools gather to refine their teaching strategies, the focus traditionally rests on textbooks, grammar drills and classroom educators. But at a recent weekend summit in Japan, a fresh voice took center stage in the effort to preserve Korean culture among the next generation: the parents. Responding to direct feedback from the local Korean diaspora, the Overseas Koreans Agency joined hands with the Kansai Association of Korean Language Schools to host an innovative three-day training workshop in Osaka on Friday and Saturday. For decades, weekend Korean schools across Japan have served as cultural anchors for "Zainichi" — ethnic Koreans who settled in Japan primarily during the colonial era, along with their descendants. Today, Japan's Ministry of Justice registers more than 400,000 ethnic Korean residents, with the total Zainichi community estimated at around 1 million when including naturalized citizens and those with Japanese nationality. item.title: Appeals court reduces ex-special counsel's sentence to 6 years in bribery case
item.description: An appellate court on Wednesday reduced former special counsel Park Young-soo's sentence on bribery-related charges by one year to six years in prison. The Seoul High Court also fined Park 200 million won ($150,000) and ordered him to forfeit 200 million won after finding him guilty of accepting the same amount from a private developer for campaign funds in his bid for the head of the Korean Bar Association. The court acknowledged the transactional nature of the exchange, noting the developer had asked Park, who then served as Woori Bank's board chair, for the bank to join talks on a consortium for the Daejang-dong property project in Seongnam, south of Seoul. A lower court had sentenced Park to seven years in prison after convicting him of accepting 300 million won from the developer. The appellate court found him guilty of accepting only 200 million won, citing inconsistencies in the developer's testimony on the rest of the amount. item.title: Korea expands farm technology support for war-scarred South Sudan
item.description: Korean peacekeepers deployed under the United Nations Mission in South Sudan are leveraging advanced agricultural science to help improve food security in one of the country's most vulnerable regions. The initiative, led by Korea’s Rural Development Administration in partnership with the military’s Hanbit Unit, integrates high-yield crop technologies into civil-affairs operations to help local communities work toward long-term agricultural self-sufficiency. Rather than relying solely on short-term food aid, Korean agricultural experts are embedding field-tested farming techniques into military civil assistance, establishing a scalable model for military-led development assistance. South Sudan, which gained independence in 2011 following decades of conflict, continues to suffer from severe food insecurity compounded by seasonal flooding, internal instability and economic shocks. item.title: American 'haenyeo' finds her place in Jeju's diving community
item.description: SEOGWIPO, Jeju Island — For American Kylie Genter, a day at the beach is no longer a day off for sunbathing and swimming. Instead, it is a place where she prays for her safety before diving into the waters to gather abalone and shellfish for living. What others see as a holiday destination has become, to her, a workplace and a landscape of possibilities. Since she began diving as a "haenyo" with fellow women divers in January 2024, the work has changed how she sees the sea. Finding her place Genter arrived in Korea as an English teacher in 2012. She moved to Jeju in 2016. While working as a tour guide, she received many questions about haenyeo and that prompted her to enroll in a diving school in 2018. She eventually took up the work after learning that Youngrak village was recruiting younger divers. “When I first started, they didn’t really know my name,” she said during a recent interview with The Korea Times. item.title: China says it is 'safeguarding order' around Taiwan-controlled South China Sea atoll
item.description: BEIJING — China's government said on Wednesday that its coast guard was "safeguarding order" around a tiny and strategically located Taiwan-controlled atoll at the top end of the South China Sea where Taipei fears Beijing is trying to enforce jurisdiction. China, which views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, said last week that Taiwan must "bear the consequences" of its coast guard using a water cannon against a Chinese fishing boat near the Pratas Islands. Taiwan has reported two incidents since Sunday of Chinese coast guard vessels approaching the Pratas, accusing Beijing of provocative behaviour. Speaking at a regular news briefing, a spokesperson for China's Taiwan Affairs Office said Beijing has "indisputable sovereignty" over the South China Sea islands, including the Pratas and their adjacent waters. "Mainland coast guard vessels conducting law enforcement patrols in the relevant waters are fulfilling their duties in accordance with the law, safeguarding normal navigation and operational order," spokesperson Zhang Han told reporters. item.title: Home of ex-election watchdog chief raided over improper overseas trip
item.description: A special counsel team on Wednesday raided the home of a former National Election Commission (NEC) chief over allegations he took improper overseas trips during his time in office. Investigators from special counsel Lee Tae-han's team searched Roh Tae-ak's home and seized a cell phone and other evidence as part of their probe into various alleged irregularities at the election watchdog. Roh has been accused of taking his wife on three overseas business trips using the NEC's money during his time in office from May 2022 until June this year, when he resigned over widespread ballot shortages in the June 3 local elections. Lee's team said it launched the raid after detecting falsehoods in official reports written by an NEC official on the outcome of the trips. Twelve personnel were mobilized in the search, including two prosecutors and seven investigators. The search warrant listed charges of embezzlement, the falsification of official documents and their use. item.title: Corporate profits, debts improve in 2025: BOK
item.description: South Korean companies' profitability and debts improved last year, driven by strong performance in the semiconductor, transportation and other industries, although their sales growth slowed, central bank data showed Wednesday. Corporate sales growth slowed to 2.4 percent last year from the previous year's 3.7 percent, according to the data from the Bank of Korea (BOK). The data is based on a review of some 983,000 non-financial firms subject to external audits. By sector, manufacturing businesses saw their sales grow by 2.4 percent in 2025, slowing from a 4.6 percent gain the previous year. Sales in the non-manufacturing sector advanced 2.3 percent last year, also slowing from a 2.9 percent advance the previous year. The ratio of local firms' combined operating profits to sales stood at 5.2 percent last year, improving from the previous year's 4.6 percent and the highest number since 2021. The firms' average debt-to-equity ratio stood at 116.2 percent last year, down from 119.9 percent the previous year and the lowest since 2019, the latest findings showed. item.title: Cosmax joins Harvard-affiliated hospital network to pursue anti-aging, metabolic research
item.description: Cosmax Group is moving beyond cosmetics into medical and biotechnology research through an expanded partnership with a Harvard-affiliated hospital network, targeting potential treatments and health products for aging, weight management and metabolic health. The Korean cosmetics manufacturer said Tuesday it signed an agreement Oct. 13 in Boston with Mass General Brigham (MGB) to launch the second phase of their joint microbiome research, known as the VIVA project. The partnership builds on research conducted from 2024 to 2026 that identified how a substance derived from certain microorganisms eased symptoms in an atopic dermatitis model and improved skin barrier function, according to Cosmax. The findings were published in Allergy, an international journal covering allergy and clinical immunology, and Cosmax has filed a Korean patent application related to the microbial technology. Under the second phase, running from 2026 through 2029, the companies plan to broaden their work beyond cosmetic ingredients to functional ingredients for health supplements and potential drug candidates. item.title: Share of irregular workers hits highest level since 2003 in Aug.: data
item.description: The proportion of irregular workers among South Korea's wage earners reached a record high of 38.5 percent in August, the data ministry said Wednesday, with their wage gap with regular workers also reaching a new record. The total number of irregular workers came to 8.67 million as of August, up from 8.56 million a year earlier, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics. South Korea conducts an annual survey on employment types among the country's economically active population based on figures from every August. The percentage of irregular salaried employees in the country's workforce was up from 38.2 percent tallied in 2025, the report showed. An official from the ministry said both the number and proportion of irregular workers reached their highest levels since South Korea began compiling related data under the current method in 2003. Male workers accounted for 3.7 million of the irregular workers, while the number of female workers came to 4.96 million. item.title: Olive Young launches K-pop live shopping show with NMIXX as 1st guest
item.description: CJ Olive Young, Korea’s largest health and beauty retail chain, said Wednesday it is launching “Green Room,” a live shopping show that combines a music talk show with live commerce, in which products are sold in real time during a livestream. The show is the retailer’s first K-pop program on Olive Young Live, its live commerce platform. Built around the idea of an artist’s waiting room before a performance, the show has a host invite artists who have recently released new music to introduce their albums and share stories from behind the scenes. Viewers can chat with the artists in real time and buy albums that come with extras sold only through Olive Young. The show will stream at the same time on Olive Young Live, the retailer’s YouTube channel, and O.Y LIVE on its Japanese-language global online mall, with real-time translation for viewers in Japan. The first episode airs at 8 p.m. Wednesday. A member of the boy band BTOB will host, and four members of girl group NMIXX will appear as guests. item.title: Genon expands in Indonesia after successful Nike production validation
item.description: Artificial intelligence (AI) solutions company Genon is expanding its manufacturing automation business in Indonesia after passing production validation for Nike footwear inspections and securing follow-on projects covering additional quality checks and robotic automation. The company said Wednesday that its AI vision inspection system detected defects in Nike outsoles with accuracy rates of 99.7 percent and 99.2 percent across two footwear styles, clearing final validation for Nike footwear production. Genon began developing the system last year, using high-resolution industrial cameras and specialized lighting to capture product surfaces, which AI analyzes to identify defects and classify products according to quality standards. The validation was designed to assess performance in real production conditions, rather than merely test technical capabilities, Genon said. The company is preparing to develop production-ready models this year, with plans to deploy the technology on manufacturing lines beginning in 2027 and gradually expand its use across products and facilities. item.title: PPP slams diplomat withdrawal from Ukraine as 'emotional response'
item.description: The main opposition People Power Party (PPP) on Wednesday criticized the Lee Jae Myung government's decision to withdraw additional diplomatic personnel from Ukraine, describing the move as an "emotional response." The foreign ministry announced the decision on Tuesday, following the recall of its ambassador to Ukraine, amid an ongoing dispute over Kyiv's unilateral disclosure of the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to South Korea. PPP floor leader Jeong Jeom-sig said the withdrawal decision was difficult to understand unless the government was steering its foreign policy away from the United States and other partner nations, and toward an alignment with North Korea, China and Russia. "The government argues that the withdrawal of its diplomatic personnel is due to the threat of air strikes, but no one is going to take that at face value," Jeong said in a Facebook post. "With the war in Ukraine dragging on for more than four years, why was the (withdrawal) decision made shortly after a dispute erupted over the transfer of North Korean POWs?" he asked. item.title: 'Dislike Trump, dislike US': No exceptions among 36 countries
item.description: Views of U.S. President Donald Trump are becoming increasingly intertwined with perceptions of the United States as a country. A survey of people in 36 countries outside the U.S. found a much stronger tendency than in the past for those who trust Trump to also view the U.S. favorably. The survey also found that those who distrust the U.S. president tend to hold negative views of the country. Korea has also seen a growing link between the two assessments. The trend was displayed in a survey of citizens in 36 countries, according to Pew Research Center. The center said it had conducted similar surveys during former President Joe Biden’s administration and Trump’s first term, but the association between views of the president and perceptions of the U.S. was weaker at the time. Pew Research Center highlighted the strong correlation between evaluations of Trump in his second term and views of the U.S. The median correlation between favorability toward the U.S. and confidence in its president stood at just 0.31 during Trump’s first term in 2017 and 0.34 under Biden in 2023-2024. item.title: GDF connects Korean SMEs with diplomats to boost exports
item.description: The Global Diplomats Forum (GDF) brought together diplomatic representatives from eight countries and Korean businesses at the National Assembly in Seoul on Monday to explore ways to help small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) expand overseas. The conference was co-hosted by GDF and the Korea Strong Small Business Association (KSSBA). Diplomatic representatives from Morocco, the United Arab Emirates, Italy, Brazil, Germany, Malaysia, Uzbekistan and the Philippines presented their countries’ market conditions, investment opportunities and key industries. The participating ambassadors included Chafik Rachadi of Morocco, Jamal Abdullah Al Suwaidi of the UAE, Emilia Gatto of Italy, Fernando Pimentel of Brazil, Georg Schmidt of Germany, Dato’ Mohd Zamruni Khalid of Malaysia, Alisher Abdusalomov of Uzbekistan and Bernadette Therese Fernandez of the Philippines. About 30 diplomatic representatives attended. The conference aimed to address challenges facing Korean SMEs seeking to enter foreign markets, including limited access to market information, local business partners and distributio

item.title: Korea serves up regional street food festivals for Taiwanese visitors
item.description: Korea’s regional street food celebrations are moving onto the international stage as tourism authorities lean into global cravings for authentic Korean cuisine. The Korea Tourism Organization (KTO) said Wednesday that it is joining forces with local governments in Daegu and North Gyeongsang Province to transform regional culinary gatherings into high-profile international travel attractions. The joint initiative targets tourists arriving via regional gateways such as Daegu International Airport and Gimhae International Airport in Busan, offering direct access to the country’s southeastern region. Focusing initially on Taiwan — a key source market with a strong affinity for Korean food culture — the tourism agency’s Taipei office partnered with local travel agencies in September to launch specialized itinerary packages. The effort has already drawn 145 Taiwanese visitors who will tour the Daegu Tteokbokki Festival and the Gimcheon Kimbap Festival on Oct. 23 and 24. item.title: POSCO International earns top AAA rating for customs compliance
item.description: POSCO International, the trading and energy arm of steelmaker POSCO Group, has secured the highest rating under the country’s Authorized Economic Operator (AEO) program — a top-tier certification set to streamline customs clearance and bolster its global supply chain network. The company said Wednesday it received the AAA certification at a ceremony held at Incheon Customs, following years of improvements to its import and export management systems. The AEO program, established under World Customs Organization standards, evaluates companies on regulatory compliance, internal controls, financial soundness and security management, assigning ratings of A, AA or AAA. POSCO International first earned an A rating in 2013 before advancing to AA in 2022, continuing to refine its trade processes and internal oversight before achieving the top tier this year. The company handles about 40,000 import and export customs declarations annually, making faster clearance procedures a potential source of greater logistics efficiency and lower operating costs. item.title: 'Smart camp' system built at Hanbit Unit in South Sudan
item.description: The Army said Wednesday it has built a "smart camp" system using advanced technology at a military base of the Hanbit Unit deployed in South Sudan for a U.N. peacekeeping mission in an effort to enhance the safety of troops. A smart camp is an advanced system that integrates various functions needed to operate a military base, such as surveillance and facilities management, by applying information and communications technology (ICT). A ceremony marking the establishment of a smart camp was held Tuesday (local time) at the Hanbit Unit base in South Sudan, marking the first of its kind among U.N. peacekeeping operation bases, according to the Army. The move is expected to enhance the safety and operational efficiency of peacekeeping troops as well as reduce harm on the environment. item.title: Samsung Bioepis wins FDA Fast Track for 1st anticancer drug candidate
item.description: Samsung Bioepis has received Fast Track designation from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for SBE303, an anticancer drug candidate based on antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) technology, the company said Wednesday. SBE303 is the first novel drug candidate in Samsung Bioepis' pipeline. It is an ADC, a type of biopharmaceutical drug designed to deliver powerful cancer-killing agents directly to cancer cells while minimizing damage to healthy tissues. ADCs are oftentimes referred to as "biological missiles" because of their targeted approach. SBE303 targets Nectin-4, a cell adhesion protein expressed in several types of cancer, including urothelial, lung and breast cancers. Existing ADCs targeting Nectin-4 face limitations because of their narrow therapeutic window, meaning the difference between an effective dose and a dose that causes serious side effects is relatively small. Samsung Bioepis designed SBE303 to address these limitations by combining an antibody that specifically targets Nectin-4 with a potent anticancer agent known as a topoisomerase I inhibitor, using its own linker

item.description: Just days after announcing his departure from Moonshot AI, teen Chinese artificial intelligence prodigy Nathan Chen Guangyu seems to have found his next destination. On Tuesday, Arfur Grok, a widely-watched anonymous social media account that tracks AI talent movements in the U.S., posted that the former Moonshot AI researcher was joining Discovery Loop, an AI start-up founded by four former Google senior researchers including former chief scientist Jeff Dean. Launched just two months ago, the start-up has quickly attracted industry attention due to its star-studded founding team as well as its ambitious mission: to automate scientific research with AI. Discovery Loop has already recruited several star researchers from U.S. big tech giants, including other former Google engineers. item.description: R&B singer Crush is back with “Squeak,” a charming new duet with pop icon IU that captures the delightful awkwardness of falling in love — marking his first solo release in more than a year. Set to be released Wednesday at 6 p.m., the single follows his August 2025 EP “FANG” and its lead track, “UP ALL NITE,” featuring SUMIN. In an interview ahead of the release, Crush discussed the song’s creation, his collaboration with IU and his hopes for the music he leaves behind. Q.
