item.title: Korea targets 170 ticket scalpers in 1st mass police referral
item.description: Under newly tightened anti-scalping laws, Korean authorities referred 170 high-volume ticket resellers to police on Wednesday, targeting an illegal trade estimated at more than 1 billion won ($770,000). The sweep marks the first major enforcement action under amended legislation that bans reselling tickets above face value, regardless of whether automated buying software was used. The move follows an unprecedented wave of public tips: Between Aug. 28, when the law took effect, and Oct. 1, authorities received over 68,000 complaints — averaging roughly 2,000 a day, a seventeenfold surge compared to last year. Cooperating with online secondary ticket platforms, regulators blocked around 30,000 suspicious posts and obtained transaction data to identify the most severe offenders. The suspects, comprising 121 sellers in sports and 49 in entertainment, allegedly offered 11,032 tickets. item.title: Teen drug offenders caught in Jan.-July near 80% of 2025 total
item.description: The number of teenagers apprehended by police for drug-related offenses in the first seven months of this year reached nearly 80 percent of last year's annual total, a lawmaker said Wednesday, citing data from the Korean National Police Agency. According to the police data released by Rep. Kim Jun-hyuk of the ruling Democratic Party, 370 teenagers were apprehended for drug offenses between January and July, equivalent to 78.7 percent of the 470 teenagers apprehended for such offenses throughout last year. The number of teenage drug offenders stood at 309 in 2021 and 294 in 2022, but surged to 1,066 in 2023. It subsequently decreased to 442 in 2024 before rising again to 470 last year. The total number of drug offenders rose from 10,626 in 2021 to 12,387 in 2022 and 17,817 in 2023. The number then fell to 13,512 in 2024 and 13,353 last year, while 8,426 offenders were apprehended in the first seven months of this year. Students accounted for a significant share of those apprehended. As of July this year, 295 students had been apprehended for drug offenses, or 63 percent of the 468 students

item.title: Former 'Produce X 101' contestant Kang Hyun-soo starts new career as civil servant
item.description: Kang Hyun-soo, a former contestant on Mnet’s "Produce X 101", has embarked on a new career as a civil servant. A recent TJB News report featured newly appointed civil servants in Boryeong, South Chungcheong Province, drawing attention to Kang, who previously pursued a career as an idol singer. While looking for a stable career, Kang studied electrical engineering under the influence of his family and decided to pursue a position in public service. He currently works in the Waterworks Division at Boryeong City Hall, where he is learning the ropes of his new job. In an interview, Kang expressed satisfaction with his new workplace. “Everyone kindly explains everything to me, and I feel like I have reliable colleagues by my side. It feels like I’ve found a place where I belong," he said. “I really like having a clear sense of belonging." Born in 1996, Kang has made three debut attempts throughout his career. item.title: BTS to kick off first-ever Peru concerts as Lima rolls out 'BTS Avenue'
item.description: Global K-pop sensation BTS will launch its first-ever concerts in Peru on Wednesday (local time), as the capital Lima rolled out a weeklong "BTS Avenue" and purple-lit landmarks to honor the group's historic visit. BigHit Music said the septet will perform at Estadio San Marcos in Lima on Wednesday, Friday and Saturday as part of its "Arirang" world tour. It marks the band's first shows in the South American country since its 2013 debut. To mark the occasion, the city's Santiago de Surco district temporarily renamed Sacramento Street as "BTS Avenue" from Oct. 5-11, installing signs along the route. Arco Morisco, a landmark structure in the district's Friendship Park, was illuminated in the group's signature color of purple on Monday and will host daily light shows through Sunday, while the Fountain of Fantasy at Lima's Fountain Park will run a BTS-themed show with music, lights and water screens during the same period. BTS opened the South American leg of the tour with two-day shows at Estadio Nemesio Camacho El Campin in Bogota last weekend, attracting around 100,000 fans.

item.title: Sejong University ranks 8th in Korea, 281st globally in THE World University Rankings 2027
item.description: Sejong University ranked eighth in Korea and 281st globally in the Times Higher Education (THE) World University Rankings 2027. With an overall score of 55.8 points, the university placed among the top 10 of the 44 Korean universities evaluated by the U.K.-based rankings agency. The university, which was listed in the 251-300 band last year, ranked 281st globally this year among the 2,297 universities evaluated worldwide. Sejong University said the results reflected its strong performance in the research quality category. It received 90.5 points in the category, the highest among Korean universities. The university became the only Korean university to score above 90 in the category, highlighting its strength in research quality. The category assesses factors including citation impact, which reflects the number of citations per publication; research strength measured by Field-Weighted Citation Impact; research excellence, which evaluates the proportion of a university’s publications among the top 10 percent of the most cited papers; and research influence. item.title: Police officer indicted for fabricating, distributing deepfake videos of acquaintances
item.description: A police officer in Seoul has been indicted for using artificial intelligence (AI) to create and spread deepfake videos of people he knew, prosecutors said Wednesday. The Busan District Prosecutors Office said the officer, stationed at Seoul's Dongdaemun Police Station, manufactured roughly 400 such videos and distributed about 50 of them between March 2022 and August this year. He was earlier arrested and detained by investigators from the Busan Metropolitan Police Agency, following a monthslong undercover investigation launched in December 2025 to verify suspicions that illegal, exploitative videos were being circulated via Telegram. The police officer was later found to have been probed for a similar offense before joining the police, but the prosecution decided against indicting him at that time. The officer was also charged with possessing about 5,600 illegally filmed videos, including about 1,600 that involve child abuse, and producing about 10 illegally filmed videos using his mobile phone.

item.title: FDI notifications in Korea rise 10.8 % in Q3
item.description: Foreign direct investment (FDI) notifications in Korea rose 10.8 percent in the third quarter from a year earlier, driven by strong global demand for Korean semiconductors and equipment for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, government data showed Wednesday. FDI notifications reached $22.9 billion in the July-September period, while FDI arrivals jumped 30.6 percent to $14.87 billion, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources said in a press release. "Korea's strong economic fundamentals appear to have helped attract foreign direct investment despite uncertainties stemming from prolonged tensions in the Middle East," the ministry said. FDI notifications for building or expanding manufacturing facilities accounted for 80 percent of the total, or $18.52 billion, with the remainder going toward mergers and acquisitions (M&As). FDI notifications from the United States jumped 35.1 percent to $6.69 billion in the third quarter. item.title: Unification Church foundation sought to sell $39 mil. in assets during probe: lawmaker
item.description: The Unification Church foundation tried to dispose of assets worth 52.3 billion won ($39 million) while it was under investigation over corruption charges linked to former President Yoon Suk Yeol, a lawmaker said Wednesday. The Foundation for the Support of HSA-UWC, run by the Unification Church, filed two applications with the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism in December and March to dispose of its land and buildings, but both were rejected, Rep. Jin Sun-mee of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea said, citing reports submitted by the ministry. By law, nonprofit organizations, such as religious foundations, must obtain approval from the ministry before disposing of their core assets, including land and buildings. The foundation applied in December to dispose of assets worth about 52 billion won in Seoul. The ministry rejected the request, however, saying there was insufficient justification for selling high-value assets without a specific plan for their use at a time when the foundation and its affiliates were under investigation by a special counsel and police. item.description: North Korea appears to be taken aback by South Korea's investigation results blaming Pyongyang for a recent mine blast near the inter-Korean border and its subsequent mine-clearing operation in the area, Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul said Wednesday. item.title: Finance minister pledges to create favorable biz environment amid challenges
item.description: Korea will work to create a favorable business environment to support economic growth while addressing structural challenges, such as stagnant productivity, the finance minister said Wednesday. Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il made the remarks during a meeting with representatives of Korea's six major business lobbies, including SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won, who heads the Korea Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KCCI). "Recently, the Korean economy has gained growth momentum despite a challenging economic environment, driven by the global semiconductor upcycle," Lee said in his opening remarks. "However, structural challenges, such as a shrinking working-age population and stagnant productivity, have weakened growth potential, while disparities across various areas persist amid growing pressures on people's livelihoods, including rising consumer prices," Lee added. Lee said the government will listen closely to businesses and work with the private sector to deliver tangible results with its policies. item.title: Trump to speak to Putin on plague as US, UN urge transparency
item.description: WASHINGTON — US President Donald Trump said Tuesday he would speak very soon with Russian President Vladimir Putin over the reported plague death of a laboratory technician, as Washington and the United Nations called for transparency from Moscow. Russian authorities denied that they were imposing anti-plague measures and played down the reports of an incident at a plague research institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region last week. But Washington is showing growing concern, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio calling on Russia to be open about the situation. The World Health Organization issued a similar appeal Tuesday. "We encourage Russia to be transparent and share more information with the world so that all of us could react accordingly and appropriately," Rubio said during a trip to Iceland. Trump later said he would be speaking to Putin about what happened. "I have a call scheduled, yes," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he had spoken to Putin on the issue yet, adding that it would happen "very soon." item.title: California couple arrested on child abuse charges in horrifying surrogacy probe
item.description: LOS ANGELES — An extremely wealthy Chinese immigrant and his wife amassed a brood of 21 children through a surrogacy scheme and raised them in a “house of horrors,” prosecutors alleged Tuesday. Guojun Xuan, 66, and Silvia Zhang, 39, were arrested at their sprawling mansion in Arcadia, a city about 13 miles (20 kilometers) northeast of downtown Los Angeles. The children suffered daily beatings from cruel nannies as the couple watched over a network of surveillance cameras and laughed, according to prosecutors. The couple allegedly recruited women across the country to serve as surrogates, promising them that they were just looking for another child to grow their family. The couple face several counts of child abuse as well as conspiracy to commit child abuse, accessory after the fact and dissuading a witness, according to Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman. “This case is unprecedented. item.title: Seoul shares extend losses late Wednesday morning as tech stocks fall
item.description: Seoul shares extended losses late Wednesday morning, weighed down by declines in technology stocks despite easing concerns over high bond yields as oil prices retreated. After opening 1.11 percent lower, the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) fell 80.66 points, or 1.16 percent, to 6,860.73 as of 11:20 a.m. Local shares bucked gains on Wall Street despite easing pressure from bond yields. Global oil prices fell on easing supply concerns, while bond yields retreated from multidecade highs. Overnight, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.49 percent, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite gained 0.45 percent to reach a record high. Institutions and foreigners sold a net 313.14 billion won ($233 million) and 1.16 trillion won worth of stocks, respectively. Individuals bought a net 1.19 trillion won. Tech stocks led the decline in Seoul. Market bellwether Samsung Electronics fell 0.28 percent, and its chipmaking rival SK hynix declined 2.09 percent. item.title: Appeals court acquits ex-President Yoon in 'free opinion polls' case
item.description: An appellate court overturned a lower court ruling Wednesday, acquitting former President Yoon Suk Yeol of charges related to receiving free opinion polls ahead of the 2022 presidential election in violation of the political funds law. The Seoul High Court found Yoon not guilty of violating the Political Funds Act, which bans improper political donations, reversing the Seoul Central District Court's conviction in July that had sentenced him to two years in prison. Following the appellate ruling, special counsel Min Joong-ki's team indicated it would file an appeal to the Supreme Court, while Yoon's legal team welcomed the acquittal. Yoon had been indicted on charges of colluding with his wife and receiving 58 opinion polls worth about 270 million won ($202,000) in total for free from self-proclaimed power broker Myung Tae-kyun between April 2021 and March 2022. item.title: Global IBs raise Korea's growth outlooks on chip boom
item.description: Major global investment banks (IBs) have upgraded their forecasts for South Korea's economic growth, citing a strong semiconductor upcycle, a report by the international finance center said Wednesday. According to the report by the Korea Center for International Finance (KCIF), the median growth forecast by major foreign institutions for 2026 was raised to 3.5 percent in September from 3.3 percent made in August. They have been upping their growth forecasts for the Korean economy since April this year. The average forecast stood at 2 percent at the end of last year. It rose to 2.1 percent in January, 2.4 percent in April and 2.8 percent in May. The upward revisions reflect expectations that the global semiconductor cycle will remain stronger and more resilient than previously anticipated. Among IBs, JP Morgan expects the Korean economy to grow 4 percent this year, up 0.2 percentage point from a month earlier. Citi jacked up its growth forecast to 3.8 percent from 3.7 percent over the cited period, according to the report. UBS also raised its forecast to 3.5 percent from 2.8 percent. For next

item.title: In interview, US Vice President Vance says Iran must cut enrichment to end war
item.description: FAIRBANKS, Alaska — US Vice President JD Vance said in an exclusive interview with Reuters that Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the countries’ seven-month war, even as Washington was unsure how Tehran makes decisions in negotiations. Vance, a longtime skeptic of US involvement in foreign wars, has taken a leading role in negotiating a settlement to the conflict and brokered a provisional peace agreement in September that quickly fell apart. The war has jolted global energy markets and become a political liability for President Donald Trump and fellow Republicans ahead of November midterm elections. Speaking on Monday after a campaign trip in Alaska, Vance said any agreement would require Iran to reduce its nuclear enrichment capacity, rather than offer assurances of future nuclear drawdowns. item.title: S. Korea's Nuri space rocket lifts off from Naro Space Center
item.description: South Korea launched its homegrown Nuri rocket Wednesday on its fifth flight to place 15 satellites into orbit, including five that will form part of the country's first domestically launched microsatellite constellation. The 200-ton Nuri blasted off from the Naro Space Center in Goheung, about 400 kilometers southwest of Seoul, at 12:25 p.m. The payload consists of five New-space Earth Observation Satellite Constellation for National Safety (NEONSAT) microsatellites and 10 CubeSats. Nuri's first and second stages will separate about 123 and 268 seconds after liftoff, respectively, with satellite deployment beginning between 810 and 960 seconds at an altitude of around 575 kilometers. The five NEONSATs, Nos. 2 through 6, will be deployed at intervals of 35 to 40 seconds, with Nuri's upper stage rotating by about 45 degrees between each separation to prevent collisions. The 10 CubeSats will then be deployed two at a time at 10-second intervals. After releasing all 15 satellites, Nuri will perform a collision-avoidance maneuver and vent its remaining fuel, completing its flight about 20 min

item.title: Korea's $449 bil. crypto economy leads in East Asia: Chainalysis
item.description: Korea's digital asset economy reached $449.1 billion from July 2025 to June 2026, the largest in East Asia, data showed Tuesday, as retail investors increasingly turned to artificial intelligence (AI)-related cryptocurrencies. According to global blockchain data platform Chainalysis' report, "East Asia Crypto Adoption Report: South Korea's AI Trade Comes to Crypto," Korea's crypto economy grew 12.3 percent from the previous one-year period to record $449.1 billion. Japan followed at $228.3 billion, with Hong Kong at $192.2 billion, China at $176.3 billion and Taiwan at $140.4 billion. The growth came largely from Korea's retail-driven crypto market, even amid limited participation by major financial institutions. The report highlighted AI-related cryptocurrencies as one of the clearest signs of that retail enthusiasm. As Korean investors piled into shares of Samsung Electronics and SK hynix amid an AI-fueled stock market rally, they also poured money into digital assets linked to AI-focused projects and infrastructure. item.title: At 94, Korea's oldest university president is still planning for future
item.description: At an age when most people have long stepped away from professional life, Lee Gil-ya is still thinking about what comes next. The 94-year-old president of Gachon University is Korea’s longest-serving university president. Lee took over the management of Kyungwon University in 1998 and became its president in 2000, later overseeing the integration of four institutions that culminated in the launch of Gachon University in 2012. She has since led the integrated university for nearly 14 years — an unusually long tenure in Korea, where university presidents typically serve relatively short terms. She attributes her forward-looking approach to decades spent building hospitals and educational institutions, where successes and failures alike taught her to recognize change early and act quickly — an approach now shaping Gachon University’s push to stay ahead in the artificial intelligence (AI) era. “Hardship itself is a kind of success. It becomes the foundation for success,” Lee said in a recent interview with The Korea Times, stressing that failures and setbacks are experiences peo

item.title: GM Korea's multi-brand strategy falls short on localization
item.description: General Motors (GM) Korea’s decision to bring to market its first Buick model — imported entirely from China — is putting its multi-brand strategy at odds with its commitment to local production, experts and industry officials said Tuesday. Last week, the carmaker unveiled Buick, positioning the premium brand as a key pillar of the strategy to offer consumers a wider range of products, along with its other brands, such as GMC, Cadillac and Chevrolet. But since Buick’s first model, the Electra E7 plug-in hybrid electric vehicle (PHEV), will be imported from China, the latest decision has also renewed questions about GM Korea’s long-term commitment to domestic production. In March, GM Korea announced a $600 million (806 billion won) investment plan to expand its production infrastructure. At a media briefing, GM Korea CEO Hector Villarreal highlighted the benefits of operating multiple brands and providing customers with greater choice. But when asked whether Buick or other new models could eventually be produced in Korea, Villarreal did not offer a specific commitment. Kim Pil-so

item.title: Cornell brings in ex-Justice official to review school's handling of sex assault claims
item.description: ITHACA, N.Y. — A former high-ranking Department of Justice official will look at how Cornell handles sexual misconduct complaints, university trustees announced Tuesday as they tried to address an outpouring of anger over allegations of a 2024 gang rape at a fraternity house. Sally Yates, who was a deputy attorney general in the Obama administration, will spearhead the review, the trustees said in an announcement. The assessment is to include how the Ivy League university investigates reports of sexual assault and sexual harassment, what support students get, how the disciplinary process works, campus police responses and oversight of fraternities, sororities and other student organizations. The announcement comes after days of outrage and demonstrations over Cornell’s response to a complaint from a woman known publicly only as Jane Doe, who told campus police in November 2024 that she had been sexually assaulted by multiple Chi Phi fraternity brothers the month before after being pressured into drinking and taking drugs. item.title: The world has nearly burned through its oil stockpile buffer, executives say
item.description: LONDON — The amount of oil in storage that is accessible to the global market is running low, industry executives said at a forum in London this week, making the market more fragile and putting upward pressure on prices. Governments and energy companies have drawn oil from stockpiles to alleviate pressure in a global oil market facing unprecedented supply disruptions this year due to the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine. "Less than 6 billion barrels of commercial inventories remain today, with the vast majority not practically available, so the system is already straining," Amin Nasser, CEO of Saudi Arabia's state oil company Saudi Aramco, said at the Energy Intelligence Forum in London. More than 1 billion barrels of oil have been released mainly from onshore commercial inventories since the start of this year's Middle East crisis, which was the last major tool in the box, Nasser said. item.title: French riot police fire tear gas as more than 250,000 rally nationwide for school funding
item.description: PARIS — Police fired tear gas to control crowds in Paris and elsewhere in France on Tuesday as more than a quarter of a million people rallied nationwide to support school pupils demanding more education funding, according to government figures. The protests increased pressure on the administration of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron. As pupils again blockaded high schools, large crowds waving flags and placards gathered in Marseille, Strasbourg and other cities. The demonstrations showed how protests that began at a high school in the Paris region in mid-September have grown into a nationwide movement — the latest of many that have marked Macron’s nearly decade-long tenure. “We need to listen to them,” said Léa Monimart, a demonstrator in the northern city of Lille. “They are 17 years old; they are not completely clueless, and they know what they are talking about. item.description: LOS ANGELES — President Donald Trump suggested to a crowd of his supporters in Nebraska that Iran could "take out" a major U.S. city like Los Angeles or San Diego, drawing a swift rebuke from California's Democratic leaders and some fellow Republicans. item.title: Ukraine says S. Korea exports eased Russia fuel crisis caused by drone strikes
item.description: LONDON/SEOUL —Russia imported more than 176,000 tons of petroleum products from South Korean ports in July and August, easing the impact of a fuel crisis caused by Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, Ukraine's top sanctions official said on Tuesday. The supplies from South Korea made up 31 percent of Russian fuel imports in August, according to the official, Vladyslav Vlasiuk, citing what he said were reports that tankers, including ones under Western sanctions, were used for the deliveries. "These shipments began precisely when Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries were reducing processing volumes and creating a fuel shortage within Russia," Vlasiuk, presidential commissioner for Ukrainian sanctions policy, wrote on Facebook. His comments come amid a diplomatic row between Seoul and Kyiv that erupted last month when President Volodymyr Zelenskiy announced the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, a step that Seoul says was meant to stay secret. Unconfirmed media reports said a major fuel depot in the Moscow region was on fire after the attack that killed two people. item.title: Wall Street rallies toward an all-time high
item.description: NEW YORK — The U.S. stock market is closing in on an all-time high on Tuesday. The S&P 500 climbed 0.8 percent and is on track to finish the day above its record closing level set in August. Even with worries about war , high inflation and cranked-up pressure from the bond market continuing to weigh on it, the backbone of many 401(k) accounts has soared nearly 24 percent since hitting a bottom in late March. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 343 points, or 0.7 percent, as of noon Eastern time, while the Nasdaq composite was adding 0.8 percent to its own all-time high set the day before. The record-high stock prices are helping investors feel better about their finances, or at least less bad, when Americans are generally feeling more discouraged about keeping up with the fast-rising cost of living. Many of the fears that sent the U.S. stock market to its bottom in March, sparked by the war with Iran , have indeed come true. Oil prices have jumped, which has made inflation worse. item.title: What do we know about plague institute lab worker's death in Russia?
item.description: MOSCOW/LONDON — A laboratory worker at a plague research institute in Siberia fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances on October 2, prompting authorities to quarantine about 200 people and causing public health fears on social media. Here's what we know about the case, which officials have not linked to her work or plague, and about the disease she studied. What happened? Russian media named the victim as Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. The authorities said she died of an unknown type of pneumonia but that as a precaution they quarantined everyone who had come into contact with her. Unconfirmed reports of how she fell ill have circulated on social media. One version said she had dropped a test tube containing live bacteria at work, a theory rejected by Russia's health watchdog. Another said she became sick after travelling to Thailand. A third said she fell ill after going to an area near the border with Mongolia. There is no evidence in the public domain to support any of those theories. Did

item.title: Trump orders firing squad for gunman who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas
item.description: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump has ordered the use of a firing squad to execute the former U.S. Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree the gunman later described as retaliation for U.S. wars in the Muslim world, the Pentagon said on Monday. Putting former U.S. Army Major Nidal Hasan to death by Army firing squad was approved by Trump at the recommendation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said on X. Parnell noted that Hasan shouted "Allahu Akbar" — God is greatest in Arabic — during the attack, which killed 12 unarmed active-duty soldiers and a retired serviceman, and wounded 32 others. The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution, Parnell said, adding, "Judgment day for Hasan has finally come." Death by firing squad was one of several forms of capital punishment the Trump administration recently added to permissible forms of execution for the gravest of federal crimes, along with electrocution and gas asphyxiation. item.title: Skipping showers before a date? What's behind 'pheromone maxxing' trend
item.description: Click here for more articles by Kormedi.com. For most people, getting ready for a date means taking a shower and perhaps putting on deodorant or perfume. But some are doing the opposite, deliberately avoiding showers and scented products in the belief that preserving their natural body odor could make them more attractive. The practice, known as "pheromone maxxing," has recently gained attention on social media, particularly among young men. The idea is to reduce showering and avoid deodorant, perfume and other fragranced products so that the body's natural scent remains as strong as possible. The trend centers on pheromones, chemical signals released by an individual that trigger specific responses in other members of the same species. Pheromones are well established in many animals and can play an important role in mating behavior. Female silkworm moths, for example, release a sex pheromone called bombykol that can attract males even at extremely low concentrations. Mice also use chemical cues in urine and other secretions to gather information about other animals, including their sex

item.title: Forget waking up at dawn: Young Koreans are embracing 'sleep maxxing'
item.description: Forget waking up before dawn to squeeze in another hour of self-improvement. For a growing number of young Koreans, getting ahead now means getting better sleep. The "miracle morning" trend, which encouraged people to wake up early and devote the extra hours to exercise, studying and other forms of self-development, once swept through Korea. Now, a contrasting wellness trend known as "sleep maxxing" is drawing attention among younger generations. The term combines "sleep" with "maxxing," internet slang for maximizing or optimizing something. Rather than simply trying to sleep longer, followers seek to improve sleep quality by systematically adjusting everything from daily habits to their bedroom environment. Kang, a 30-year-old office worker, is among those willing to spend money in pursuit of a better night's sleep. A smartwatch tracks total sleep time and the proportion of deep sleep, while supplements are part of a routine aimed at relaxation. A sleep mask and earplugs have also become bedtime essentials. "There were many days when I was exhausted but couldn't actually fall asleep onc

item.title: Three Years into Genocide, "The IDF Is Still Hunting Gazans": Palestinian Journalist Akram al-Satarri
item.description:
In Gaza, October 7, 2023, is viewed as the beginning of the genocide. Over the past three years, Israel killed over 74,000 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, but many believe that number is a vast undercount. The killing continues despite a so-called ceasefire that took effect about a year ago.

“Every single aspect of the life of the people of Gaza has changed once and forever,” since October 7, says Akram al-Satarri, a Gaza-based journalist. He points out that a large majority of structures in the Gaza Strip have been reduced to rubble and that Israel controls around 70% of Gaza. “The Israeli Air Force is still hovering all around different parts of the Gaza Strip, and the IDF is still hunting Gazans, disturbing the already disturbed life, spreading death and displacement once and once again.”

item.title: "Origins of a Genocide": Al Jazeera's Marwan Bishara on "Twelve Days That Shook the Middle East"
item.description:
Twelve Days That Shook the Middle East: Origins of a Genocide is the new book by Al Jazeera senior political analyst Marwan Bishara discussing the crucial 12 days between Benjamin Netanyahu’s October 7 speech and Biden’s “rare” Oval Office speech on October 19. “October 7 was bloody, and it was horrific. … But Netanyahu and his government had to go overboard, to exaggerate, to lie, to deceive about what exactly happened” in order to justify their actions in Gaza, says Bishara. “Genocides don’t start with bombs; they start with ideology. And in this case, the ideology has been decades in the making.”

“During the Biden administration, the United States was basically complicit in genocide,” adds Bishara.

item.title: Israeli Activist Maoz Inon Lost His Parents on Oct. 7, Decries Israel's Ethnic Cleansing of Gaza
item.description:
Israelis and Palestinians are marking three years since October 7, 2023, when Hamas launched a surprise attack on Israel. Nearly 1,200 Israelis were killed, and around 250 were taken hostage. It was the deadliest such attack in Israel’s history, after which Israel immediately began bombing the Gaza Strip, killing at least 5,000 people by October 23, 2023. At least 74,000 Palestinians have been killed.

Israeli peace activist Maoz Inon lost both of his parents, who lived on a kibbutz just north of the Gaza border, in the Hamas attack. In the aftermath, Inon called for peace and reconciliation rather than revenge. He has spent much of the past three years working closely with Palestinian peace activist Aziz Abu Sarah.

“The Israeli government exploited the trauma, the pain, the fear of the Israelis after the October 7th massacre to change the status quo from conflict management to ethnic cleansing,” says Inon. “Those who choose ethnic cleansing, those who choose bloodshed, those who choose destruction must be sanctioned,” he adds.

item.title: Outrage in Japan after U.S. Marine accused of murdering Okinawan woman
item.description: A U.S. Marine was arrested this week on suspicion of robbing and killing a local woman in Okinawa. The killing has drawn outrage on the island and inflamed longstanding tensions over U.S. military bases, which residents say are a source of noise, pollution and violent crime against women.

item.title: Why thousands of high school students in France are protesting
item.description: Police fired tear gas and water cannons at protesters blockading French high schools — as students, teachers, parents and unions took to the streets against what they say is underfunding of the education system. Rights groups and students have accused authorities of using disproportionate force against minors. The government ‌has responded to the demonstrations with riot police and says the movement has been hijacked by outsiders and morphed into urban violence.

item.title: Rubio downplays prospects of any future US free trade agreements
item.description: REYKJAVIK, Iceland — U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio downplayed the prospect of the United States signing any new free trade agreements in the foreseeable future, speaking in Iceland on Tuesday. Asked about a possible trade deal with Iceland during a visit to the country, he said: "I think the era of free trade agreements for the foreseeable future is probably not going to be there — I mean, not with Iceland — just in general, writ large."

item.title: Russia tells WHO there are no plague cases in Siberian city
item.description: GENEVA — Russian authorities told the World Health Organization (WHO) on Tuesday that it has no cases of plague in the city of Irkutsk in Siberia, where a laboratory worker at a plague research institute died last week, according to a spokesperson for the UN health agency. Moscow, which is required under global health rules to respond to WHO requests within 24 hours, previously told the WHO authorities were investigating whether pneumonic plague caused her death. "No case of this dangerous disease has been recorded in the city of Irkutsk, Russian Federation," Russian authorities said in an official response to a WHO request, read out by WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier at a Geneva press briefing. They also told the UN agency they have identified the people in contact with the deceased and that test results for dangerous infectious pathogens were negative. Reuters could not immediately establish if this meant that they had also tested the laboratory worker and whether they could rule out plague in her case. The Russian diplomatic mission to the UN in Geneva did not immediately respo

item.title: Shinsegae to invest $1 bil. in Paramount's Warner Bros. deal
item.description: Retail conglomerate Shinsegae Group will invest $1 billion in Paramount Skydance’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, seeking to expand its retail business into global entertainment and content. The group announced Tuesday that its real estate and development arm, Shinsegae Property, will take a $1 billion stake in the combined company, alongside investors including Skydance co-CEO David Ellison and U.S. investment firm RedBird. The deal is expected to close Tuesday (local time). The investment will give Shinsegae Group access to intellectual property from Paramount and Warner Bros., including Hollywood blockbuster franchises such as “Mission: Impossible,” “Star Trek” and “Top Gun,” as well as “Harry Potter” and “Game of Thrones.” The group said it plans to combine its retail and entertainment businesses to build a platform that brings shopping and culture together, with ambitions to become a leading content hub in Asia. “This investment will go beyond a simple equity investment and serve as a stepping stone for Shinsegae Group to diversify into a new business

item.title: Francis Halzen wins Nobel Prize in physics for work on mysterious ghost particles called neutrinos
item.description: STOCKHOLM — Francis Halzen won the Nobel Prize in physics on Tuesday for his efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos, tiny cosmic particles that scientists believe offer clues to how the universe evolved. “It was a great surprise and I obviously didn’t expect it,” Halzen said, speaking to the committee by phone from Italy, in a call broadcast at the news conference to announce the winner. Halzen said it was predicted before that he would win the Nobel Prize but the announcement still made him feel “strange.” “I am working on a proposal, and I hope that this prize will help getting it approved,” he said to chuckles from the audience. Halzen paved the way for a new kind of astronomy The Nobel Committee for Physics also said Halzen’s work was instrumental to the construction of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica. “Francis Halzen realized that the ice at the South Pole could visualize these neutrino messengers from cosmos,” committee member Eva Olsson said during the news conference. “People joined him in the quest for these neutrino messengers. item.title: N. Korea warns of 'powerful counteraction' if S. Korea intrudes 'even a millimeter' into its territory
item.description: North Korea on Tuesday warned of an "immediate and powerful counteraction" if South Korea intrudes even "a millimeter" into its territory, after Seoul signaled corresponding measures over a recent land mine blast at the inter-Korean border that it has blamed on Pyongyang. The North's foreign ministry issued the statement a day after the South's military concluded the mines planted by North Korea caused the Sept. 21 blast on the southern side of the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that left two South Korean soldiers critically injured. The South's military also conducted a mine-clearing operation at the blast site on the same day, in coordination with the U.N. Command (UNC), which oversees the border area. "We do not care about them trying to remove the mines irrelevant to us, and we have no reason to pay heed to such farce of the ROK," the ministry said, calling South Korea by its official name, the Republic of Korea. "However, if a jackboot or a spark of fire from the ROK goes even a millimeter beyond the border to violate our territory, the border guard forces of the DPRK will take an immedia

item.title: South Korea may take North Korean mine attack issue to UN
item.description: Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said Tuesday that South Korea is considering calling on the United Nations to take action against North Korea for planting land mines south of the Military Demarcation Line (MDL). He made the remarks during a parliamentary audit of the foreign ministry, following the South Korean military concluding on Monday that North Korean troops had planted land mines south of the MDL in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ). The mines exploded on Sept. 21 and seriously injured several South Korean soldiers. The U.N. Command (UNC) determined that placing the mines violated the 1953 Korean Armistice Agreement. Cho said the government is considering imposing unilateral sanctions targeting North Korea, as well as sending a letter to the president of the U.N. Security Council (UNSC) to call for U.N.-level action. When asked what actions would be possible, Cho said, "If the issue is dealt with at the UNSC, it could lead to a statement by the UNSC chief or the adoption of a resolution. Or we could just send a letter or not do it at all ... We are reviewing all four options." Cho said hold

item.title: Celebrities who tried opening cafes in Korea say 'think twice'
item.description: Korea may look like a cafe lover's paradise, with coffee shops seemingly around every corner. But celebrities who have actually tried running one have a surprisingly sobering message for aspiring owners: Think twice. Singer and rapper Hanhae recently shared his own costly experience in the cafe business, while K-pop icon Lee Hyo-ri revealed that even the wildly popular Jeju cafe run by her husband, musician Lee Sang-soon, did not make as much money as its long lines might have suggested. The two discussed the realities of running a cafe on the Monday episode of JTBC's relationship reality show "Love War," after a woman featured on the program said she dreamed of opening one. Hanhae immediately tried to talk her out of it. "I've actually failed at running a cafe before, so this doesn't feel like someone else's problem," he said. Hanhae said he opened a small cafe in Seoul's Sangam-dong several years ago, selling yogurt and coffee. But competing on price proved difficult when a major franchise nearby was selling coffee for as little as 900 won ($0.64) per cup. He said the reality was a far c

item.title: Lee orders renewed discussions on possible membership to CPTPP
item.description: President Lee Jae Myung instructed the government Tuesday to start over discussions on whether South Korea should join the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) amid opposition from farmers and fishermen. Lee gave the order during the closed-door portion of a Cabinet meeting at Cheong Wa Dae, referring to the major Indo-Pacific trade agreement comprising 12 countries, including Japan, Mexico, Australia, Canada and Vietnam. Together, the member countries accounted for about 15.2 percent of global trade in 2019. "President Lee said there are opinions that the CPTPP's strategic value is important at a time of profound change in the international trade order, as well as opinions that the farming and fishing industries have great concerns," presidential spokesperson Kang Yu-jung said in a written briefing. "He stressed that policies should be pursued by calculating the national interest based on trust and shared understanding among farmers and fishermen, and ordered starting over conversations from scratch without rushing toward a fixed conclusion," sh

item.title: One year on, Trump's Gaza plan has not stopped Israeli fire or disarmed Hamas
item.description: JERUSALEM — U.S. President Donald Trump’s year-old plan to end the Gaza war has stalled, with Israel mounting near daily attacks and occupying around two-thirds of the shattered enclave where Palestinians face dire conditions. The initial phase resulted in a ceasefire on Oct. 10, 2025, and secured the release of the last remaining hostages seized in Hamas’ 2023 attacks on Israel, along with freedom for hundreds of Palestinian prisoners and detainees held by Israel. But other goals, including disarming Hamas, securing Israeli withdrawal and rebuilding Gaza, appear far from reach. What was in the plan? The first phase of Trump’s 20-point plan included a suspension of all military operations, Israeli withdrawal from part of the enclave, hostage and prisoner releases and a surge in aid. Later phases foresaw Hamas disarming and new governance by a Palestinian body overseen by the Trump-led Board of Peace. Israel would gradually withdraw, handing territory to a temporary International Stabilization Force (ISF). “Gaza will be redeveloped for the benefit of the people of Gaza, who have s

item.title: Is crowd surfing a thing of the past in smartphone era? K-pop idol's fall raises question
item.description: Crowd surfing once depended on a sea of raised hands. These days, many of those hands are holding smartphones. That collision between an old concert ritual and modern fan culture played out at a university festival in Seoul, where Tarzzan of K-pop coed group ALLDAY PROJECT fell to the ground after leaping backward from the stage in an apparent attempt to crowd surf. ALLDAY PROJECT performed at Konkuk University on Thursday. During the set, Tarzzan suddenly threw himself toward the audience, apparently expecting fans below to catch and carry him. But many concertgoers had their phones raised to film the performance and were unable to support him as he came down. Tarzzan ultimately fell to the ground, creating an alarming moment for both the performer and those around him. Security personnel helped him back onto the stage. Tarzzan then repeatedly checked on the audience rather than immediately turning attention to himself. "Is everyone here OK? I'm sorry. Nobody got hurt, right?" he asked. Despite the fall, he continued performing and completed the set. The incident soon spread across social

item.title: Korean won rises slightly against US dollar
item.description: The Korean won rose slightly against the U.S. dollar Tuesday, despite the broad strength in the U.S. currency amid lowered expectations about a rate hike by the Federal Reserve. The won was quoted at 1,343.6 won per dollar at 3:30 p.m., up 0.4 won from the close of the previous stock trading session. With the U.S. job market reporting a slower-than-expected growth in September, expectations were reduced for the Fed to tighten its monetary policy this month. Still, rising U.S. Treasury yields remained in focus. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield surged past 5.34 percent, marking the highest level since April 2002. Foreigners sold a net 1.7 trillion won ($1.27 billion) worth of local stocks during the latest regular trading session, with the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index falling 0.89 percent to close at 6,941.39.

item.title: Chief justice calls presidential intervention in Supreme Court nominations unconstitutional
item.description: Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae said Tuesday that the president has no authority to intervene when he recommends candidates for justices of the top court, escalating a dispute with President Lee Jae Myung over the selection of a new justice. Cho made the remarks during a parliamentary audit of the Supreme Court, where he strongly defended his constitutional authority and criticized Cheong Wa Dae's demand that he nominate another candidate. "Just as the chief justice cannot interfere in the National Assembly's approval process or the president's appointment process, neither the National Assembly nor the president can interfere in the chief justice's recommendation," Cho said. He argued that such intervention would violate the constitutional division of powers among state institutions and undermine judicial independence. His remarks followed a clash between Lee and the chief justice over the justice selection that has lasted more than a month. Under Article 104 of the Constitution, a 10-member recommendation committee selects at least three candidates for Supreme Court justice. The

item.title: Police pledge stern action against threats toward actor over film controversy
item.description: Police said Tuesday it will take stern action against threats targeting actor Yoo Hae-jin, following protests outside his home over alleged historical inaccuracies in his film "The Assassin(s)." Ko Beom-seok, head of the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency, issued such a warning during a press briefing, one day after Culture Minister Choi Hui-young asked the police to enhance safety measures for those involved in the film and take stern measures. On Sunday, conservative civic groups gathered outside the actor's home in northern Seoul to criticize the movie that allegedly implies late former President Park Chung-hee's involvement in the 1974 assassination of his own wife Yuk Yeong-su. "If we determine there is a risk to Yoo's safety, we will prepare additional measures, such as stepping up patrols or providing personal protection," Ko added. Earlier Tuesday, a civic group staged a rally in central Seoul, urging local companies to cancel their advertising contracts with Yoo. Another group of protesters gathered outside Hive Media Corp. to urge the production company to apologize to the public

item.title: SK Chemicals to turn discarded banners into new banner fabric
item.description: SK Chemicals said Tuesday it will establish a regional partnership network to recycle discarded banners into new banner fabric using its depolymerization technology as part of efforts to tackle the nation’s mounting waste problem. According to the company, it has formed a banner recycling consortium with four partners — MOA and Daehan Media in the Gyeongsang region, Upcloth in the Jeolla region and the resource-circulation team of Seogwipo City on Jeju Island — to establish a regional recycling system. The partnership comes as Korea generates about 6,000 tons of discarded banners annually, with around 70 percent ending up in landfills or being incinerated, according to the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment. Each of the targeted regions generates more than 1,000 metric tons of banner waste annually, according to the company. SK Chemicals will use its depolymerization technology as the core of the project, chemically breaking down plastic waste into molecular building blocks and converting it back into raw materials for producing new banner fabric. item.title: Humanoid robots take center stage as Seoul opens Smart Life Week
item.description: Inside the exhibition halls of Coex in southern Seoul on Tuesday, a bipedal humanoid robot swayed its arms to a K-pop beat. Across the room, another white robotic torso traded swift returns with a human opponent across a badminton net while robot fighters wearing oversized red and blue headgear sparred inside a miniature boxing ring. The spectacle marked the opening of Smart Life Week (SLW) 2026, a tech-driven smart city expo hosted by the Seoul Metropolitan Government. Running through Thursday under the theme “Designing Life with AI,” the exhibition brings together 529 participating firms, public institutions and city governments to showcase how artificial intelligence (AI) is shifting from digital screens into physical reality. This year’s event placed heavy emphasis on robotics and “physical AI,” which is capable of sensing, navigating and acting in physical environments alongside humans. item.title: Korea reaffirms Alaska LNG investment hinges on commercial viability
item.description: Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan reaffirmed Tuesday that Korea would participate in the Alaska liquefied natural gas (LNG) project only if it proves to be commercially viable, saying the government has just begun reviewing the proposal. He added, however, that while poor economics had long held the project back, the Middle East war had strengthened its strategic importance. “There is no question that weak commercial reasonableness kept the project from moving forward. But the Middle East war has created new strategic value,” Kim told lawmakers during a parliamentary audit. “If the project succeeds and Korea can secure LNG from Alaska, there would clearly be strategic benefits.” He made the comments in response to a question from Rep. Choi Soo-jin of the main opposition People Power Party. Choi accused Washington of presenting a large Korean investment as a foregone conclusion despite the project having stalled for four decades because of poor economic viability. item.title: [COVER STORY] Ukraine's apology over NK POWs falls short of Korea's expectation: foreign minister
item.description: Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said Tuesday that Ukraine sent an apology over its disclosure of the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea but the message fell short of Seoul’s expectations. He said the government is considering further diplomatic actions. Cho made the remarks during a parliamentary audit of the foreign ministry amid a dispute over Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s disclosure of the transfer, which Seoul said the two sides had agreed to keep confidential. “I have been exchanging messages with the Ukrainian foreign minister, who is very troubled by the situation, and I received a message that included words of apology,” Cho told lawmakers. “But it was somewhat different from the level we had expected, so we intend to take firm measures,” he said. item.title: Egyptian president to make state visit to Korea this week
item.description: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi will make a state visit to Korea this week and hold a summit with President Lee Jae Myung on economic and international issues, Lee's office said Tuesday. At Lee's invitation, El-Sisi will arrive in Korea on Wednesday and meet with Lee Thursday during a three-day stay, presidential spokesperson Kang Yu-jung said in a written briefing. "Through the summit, (the two leaders) plan to hold in-depth discussions on economic cooperation, such as trade and investment, infrastructure and supply chains, as well as expanding people-to-people exchanges, the regional political situation and international issues," she said. This will be El-Sisi's first visit to the country since 2016. The two men last met in November during Lee's visit to Egypt. "We expect President El-Sisi's state visit to serve as an important opportunity to develop Korea-Egypt ties into a strategic partnership and further strengthen our country's cooperation with Africa and the Middle East," Kang said.

item.title: Busan Int'l Film Festival kicks off star-studded 10-day run
item.description: BUSAN — The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) opened Tuesday for a 10-day run, bringing 316 films from 59 countries to Korea’s southeastern port city and ushering in an expanded set of cinema events with international prestige. The opening ceremony, hosted by actor Kim Min-ha, took place at the Busan Cinema Center, officially kicking off Asia’s largest film festival. Following the opening ceremony, director Kim Jong-kwan’s "The Table: Day and Night" will have its world premiere as the opening film. The movie explores the intersecting lives of four couples visiting a cafe during the transition from summer to autumn. Kim expressed his gratitude for the festival's spotlight on details, lauding their importance for his film, which weaves together four separate stories. "This movie is a story about small, subtle things, focusing on the meaning and beauty held within them," Kim said during a press conference at the Busan Cinema Center. "I am deeply honored and delighted to present this film on such a prestigious stage as the opening of the Busan International Film Festival.

item.title: Lotte Department Store tops $744 mil. in foreign customer sales
item.description: Lotte Department Store said its foreign customer sales nationwide surpassed 1 trillion won ($744 million) on Tuesday, making it the first Korean department store operator to reach the milestone. The retailer, which already exceeded last year's total of 734.8 billion won in July, attributed the growth to demand for luxury goods and Korean fashion, food and cultural experiences. Its Myeong-dong shopping district operations in central Seoul generated about 520 billion won in sales to foreign customers. The flagship store has expanded Korean fashion offerings and themed events to attract overseas visitors. Foreign customer sales at its Jamsil complex in eastern Seoul doubled from a year earlier. Shoppers from North America and Europe accounted for 35 percent of foreign sales there, up 15 percent from 2019. Growth also extended beyond Seoul. Sales to foreign shoppers at its Busan stores rose 150 percent from the previous year, while those at stores in the country’s southwestern region, including Jeonju and Gwangju, doubled during the same period, according to the company. item.title: Samsung Electro-Mechanics lands $210 mil. MLCC supply deal
item.description: Samsung Electro-Mechanics has secured a $210.24 million (282 billion won) order to supply multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) to a global company, adding to a string of large deals driven by growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) server components, the company said Tuesday in a regulatory filing. The company signed the one-year supply contract, which runs from Jan. 1 through Dec. 31, 2027. The customer was not disclosed due to a confidentiality agreement. The latest deal represents 2.5 percent of Samsung Electro-Mechanics’ total sales last year. It brings the value of the company’s major supply contracts announced this year to nearly 4 trillion won, which includes contracts not subject to disclosure. MLCCs regulate electrical current and reduce electromagnetic interference in electronic circuits. AI servers require more MLCCs than conventional servers and demand for the products goes higher under high-temperature and high-voltage conditions. item.title: Doosan Enerbility ships 1st gas turbine to US for SpaceXAI
item.description: Doosan Enerbility said Wednesday it has shipped a gas turbine to Space XAI for the U.S.-based artificial intelligence (AI) company's energy infrastructure project. The South Korean power plant builder said the DGT6-300H gas turbine was manufactured at its facility in the southeastern city of Changwon, marking the company's first gas turbine shipment to the United States. The turbine will be deployed as part of a U.S. energy infrastructure project by SpaceXAI, the AI arm of Elon Musk's SpaceX, according to the Korean company. Doosan Enerbility said it plans to expand cooperation with global technology companies amid growing demand for power generation equipment for AI infrastructure.

item.title: Korea has 52 death row inmates, average age of 58.7
item.description: With executions suspended in Korea for nearly 30 years, 52 death row inmates are currently being held in domestic correctional facilities, the justice ministry said Tuesday. The death row prisoners have an average age of 58.7, while 17, or 32.7 percent, are aged 60 or older, the ministry said, four days ahead of World Day Against the Death Penalty, observed annually on Oct. 10. Those in their 50s make up the largest group, with 29 inmates, it added. The death-sentenced prisoners include notorious serial killers Yoo Young-chul and Kang Ho-sun, who are currently imprisoned at the Seoul Detention Center after being convicted of killing 20 and 10 people, respectively. Korea has not carried out an execution for nearly 30 years, with the last execution taking place on Dec. 30, 1997, when 23 people, including members of the Jijonpa murder gang, were put to death in the final year of the Kim Young-sam administration. Amnesty International has classified Korea as a "de facto abolitionist state" since 2007. The death row population has been aging as the debate over whether to abolish the death pen

item.title: Astana AI Film Festival crowns winners, $450,000 Grand Prize goes to Latvia
item.description: Kazakhstan hosted the inaugural Astana AI Film Festival, drawing 8,067 entries from 125 countries and becoming the world’s largest international competition for artificial intelligence (AI)-generated films. The festival’s Grand Prix and $450,000 prize, equivalent to around 201.5 million tenge, went to Latvian filmmaker Nikolay Shestak for "The First Honest Day." Kazakhstan’s Myrzakhan Zhumakhan won the Best Character category for his comedy "It Was Just a Joke." The film follows a dog and its owner’s brother as they quarrel over a prank, with events unfolding like a blockbuster. Zhumakhan said he enjoys pranks and humor, which inspired him to create the story. The second-place award of $200,000, or about 89.5 million tenge, went to India’s "SITARA," while Spain’s "Looking For Perseida" took third place and $100,000, equivalent to around 44.8 million tenge. Only 25 films were selected from thousands of submissions to reach the final. item.title: Spy agency rejects media report on US visa denial for staff
item.description: Korea’s spy agency said Tuesday that it is in talks with the United States over delays in issuing visas to some of its employees scheduled to work at the Korean Embassy in Washington, denying a media report that their visa applications had been rejected. The statement from the National Intelligence Service (NIS) came in response to a Chosun Ilbo report revealing that the U.S. government had not approved Korea's request to dispatch NIS personnel to Washington as diplomats. The report also said Washington has not yet reached an agreement with Seoul over the departure of a senior NIS official who is supposed to return to Korea. “The delays in some visa applications are related to issues concerning the applicants’ personal information as part of the strengthened U.S. entry procedures,” the NIS said. “We are closely consulting with the U.S. side on the matter.” The intelligence agency further dismissed claims that the visa delays were linked to broader tensions between Seoul and Washington, including disputes over e-commerce giant Coupang and allegations involving intelligence act

item.title: Assembly speaker to embark on 4-nation trip to Europe
item.description: National Assembly Speaker Cho Jeong-sik was set to depart on a four-nation trip to Europe on Tuesday to discuss economic and industrial cooperation. Cho plans to visit Italy, Vatican City, Croatia and Greece over nine days on his first overseas trip since taking office in June. In Italy, he is scheduled to meet with Lorenzo Fontana, president of the country's Chamber of Deputies, and Gian Marco Centinaio, vice president of its Senate, on Wednesday to discuss expanding exchanges between the countries' parliaments and supporting economic and industrial cooperation. In Vatican City, he is scheduled to meet with Cardinal Pietro Parolin, secretary of state of the Holy See, and Cardinal Lazarus You Heung-sik to convey the commitment of the National Assembly to support World Youth Day 2027, which South Korea will host. Cho also plans to use the meetings to ask for the Vatican's continued attention and support for peace on the Korean Peninsula and the resumption of dialogue between South and North Korea. In Vatican City, he is scheduled to meet with Cardinal Pietro Parolin, secretary of state of the Holy See, and Cardinal Lazarus You Heung-sik to convey the commitment of the National Assembly to support World Youth Day 2027, which South Korea will host. Cho also plans to use the meetings to ask for the Vatican's continued attention and support for peace on the Korean Peninsula and the resumption of dialogue between South and North Korea. item.title: Gov't issues consumer alert, launches monthlong effort to prevent fraud after data breaches
item.description: Financial authorities issued a consumer alert at the “caution” level Tuesday after suspected artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cyberattacks stole personal information from banks, savings banks and a capital finance company. They also launched a monthlong special response period to prevent scams involving the stolen data. The measures follow data breaches reported at seven firms since the beginning of this month — Shinhan Bank, KB Kookmin Bank, Hana Bank, BNK Busan Bank, Yegaram Savings Bank, Welcome Savings Bank and Hyundai Capital. The incidents suggest the attacks, first reported in the banking sector, are having a broader impact. During the special response period, financial firms must open dedicated support channels for affected customers and immediately report any confirmed or suspected cases of fraud that may follow to regulators. Firms must also strengthen monitoring through their fraud detection systems. Suspicious information linked to the breaches will be promptly shared through an AI-powered platform for sharing and analyzing voice phishing information for financial

item.title: Bank hacking spree raises stakes for upcoming CEO reshuffle
item.description: A recent wave of cyberattacks on local banks is raising the stakes for an upcoming CEO reshuffle, with the heads of the country's five major lenders all set to see their terms expire at the end of the year, industry officials said Tuesday. The incidents, some of which involved artificial intelligence (AI), are expected to put banks' cybersecurity measures under greater scrutiny during this month's parliamentary audit and weigh on decisions over whether to reappoint incumbent chiefs. item.title: 'Reawaken Man: The Red' defies death, gravity in bold action gamble
item.description: "Reawaken Man: The Red" is action through and through. Koo Kyo-hwan, an actor who has moved fluidly across genres, takes on a new challenge by diving headfirst into action in "Reawaken Man: The Red." At a time when Korean action films have increasingly emphasized realistic combat and visceral impact, the film makes a bold choice by building its spectacle around a decidedly unrealistic premise: resurrection. Based on the popular webtoon of the same name, "Reawaken Man: The Red" follows Seok-hwan, played by Koo, an unemployed job seeker who discovers that he comes back to life 72 hours after dying. That extraordinary ability soon makes him the target of a relentless pursuit. The story builds on the idea that an ordinary man becomes increasingly powerful each time he dies and returns. At a relatively brisk 101 minutes, the film compresses its narrative into a fast-paced package that rarely slows down. Action is what gives the story much of that momentum. item.title: Robotic arms take over school kitchen duties in southern Seoul
item.description: The newest assistant in Seoul’s school kitchens doesn't take lunch breaks, doesn't mind the steam and automatically drains boiling grease after deep-frying. And according to local students, its cooking is a hit. Gangnam District in southern Seoul said Tuesday that its ongoing school meal robot program has undergone major upgrades based on feedback from school kitchen staff. The automated cooking system, first installed in August 2023 across three local schools — Gaeil Elementary, Gaewon Middle and Seoul Robotics High School — is proving that human-robot collaboration can transform high-stress workplaces. Originally launched as a pilot program with the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education and Korea Robotics — a local firm specializing in kitchen automation — the system pairs collaborative robotic arms with custom control software and heavy-duty cooking kettles. Rather than replacing kitchen staff, these mechanical assistants handle the most physically demanding tasks, from deep-frying to stirring large vats of soup and stir-fries. The safety improvements have been substantial

item.title: Hyundai Glovis, LGL explore SMR-powered car carrier route
item.description: Hyundai Glovis said Tuesday it has signed a memorandum of understanding with U.S.-based Liberty Global Logistics (LGL) to jointly explore operating a small modular reactor (SMR)-powered pure car and truck carrier (PCTC) between Korea and the United States. LGL specializes in transporting automobiles, heavy equipment, breakbulk and project cargo and is a major U.S. Department of Defense contractor for government cargo. The agreement was signed Sept. 30 at LGL's headquarters in Jericho, New York, with Kim Tae-woo, executive vice president of Hyundai Glovis' Logistics Business Division, and David Minetti, president of LGL, among the officials present from both companies. Hyundai Glovis will assess port conditions, regulations and operational requirements in Korea, while LGL will review the U.S. regulatory and operating environment. The companies will also study vessel development and construction, flag-state and classification requirements, and commercialization strategies. An SMR-powered vessel could enable long-term operations with minimal carbon emissions and without frequent refueling.

item.title: Seoul sent $2.4 bil. to Washington for Texas energy project: finance minister
item.description: Korea has transferred $2.4 billion to Washington as part of its funding for a Texas energy project agreed upon by the two countries under Seoul's investment initiative, the finance minister confirmed Tuesday. Responding to a lawmaker's question about whether the transfer had been made during a parliamentary audit, Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il replied "yes," acknowledging around 10 percent of the project's estimated budget was sent to the United States on Thursday. The gas-fired combined-cycle power plant project in Texas, dubbed "Project Star," calls for the construction of a 6,472-megawatt power plant for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers at a cost of $22.3 billion. The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources recently announced three projects under Korea's investment pledge to the U.S., unveiled last year in return for lower tariffs. The pledge comprises $150 billion for shipbuilding cooperation and $200 billion for projects in various strategic sectors. item.title: Saudi-backed Yemeni forces expel Houthi rebels from several areas around key strait, officials say
item.description: ADEN, Yemen — Forces of the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen have recaptured several key areas around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait from Iran-backed Houthi rebels , Yemeni officials said Monday, while the Houthis claimed attacks on Saudi oil facilities, airports and military bases as fighting escalated on Yemen’s western coast. The Yemeni officials said forces allied with the internationally recognized government retook the crucial town of Dhubab just north of the strait, a vital shipping route that connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. They also captured the towns of Bab and Hadeid, said the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters. Witnesses said they saw government tanks and forces entering the towns. The government push came as part of a major offensive launched early Monday under air cover by a Saudi military coalition. item.title: Busan shark refuses to leave canal for 3 weeks despite rescue attempts
item.description: Nearly three weeks have passed as of Tuesday since a shark, now the most famous of its kind in Korea, got trapped in a canal at a waterfront park in the southeastern city of Busan, despite local authorities' rescue attempts. The shark was first spotted Sept. 18 in the narrow canal at the city's North Port, located some 330 kilometers south of Seoul. For the next two days, nearly 20,000 visitors came to see the shark, a fivefold increase compared with the park's usual daily average of about 2,000 visitors during holidays. Public interest spiked dramatically during the Chuseok holiday, which fell on Sept. 25, with a daily average of 120,750 visitors flocking to the waterfront park between Sept. 24 and Sept. 27. The shark has been affectionately named "Bukang-i" after Bukhang, or North Port, as well as serving as an honorary ambassador of Busan. As of Monday, 1.02 million people have visited the park to see Bukang-i, according to the Busan city government. item.title: Seoul unveils 2026 Gourmet 100 list to map out capital's best bites
item.description: From hidden neighborhood eateries to trendy dessert spots, Seoul is offering international travelers a curated path through its culinary scene with the launch of its 2026 Gourmet 100 guide and an expanded citywide food festival. The Seoul Metropolitan Government said Tuesday that 100 restaurants and food establishments were selected across seven categories — Korean, Western, Asian, grill, vegetarian, cafe and dessert, and bars and pubs — by a panel of 60 Korean food experts. The list, launched in 2020, includes 27 Korean food establishments, 23 Western, 15 Asian, 10 grill, eight vegetarian, nine cafe and dessert, and eight bar and pub venues, with 25 newcomers this year. The 2026 selection organizes Seoul’s culinary landscape into distinct categories, spanning traditional Korean fine dining, Western cuisine, Asian flavors, Grill establishments, Plant-Based eateries, Bars & Pubs, and a newly expanded Cafe & Dessert section. item.title: FM Cho says S. Korea reviewing diplomatic responses to NK mine blast inside DMZ
item.description: Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said Tuesday that South Korea is reviewing various diplomatic measures in response to recent mine explosions inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), while seeking to prevent the situation from escalating unnecessarily. Cho made the remarks during a parliamentary audit of his ministry, a day after the Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) concluded that North Korean land mines planted south of the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) caused injuries to three South Korean soldiers inside the DMZ on Sept. 21. "We take this matter very seriously. Based on the final results of the investigation, the ministry is reviewing various things it can do and will work with the National Security Council to formulate the government's response," Cho said. The blasts occurred while South Korean troops were clearing a path for a joint inspection with the U.N. Command (UNC) to verify suspicions that Pyongyang had illegally planted land mines south of the border in violation of the Armistice Agreement that ended the 1950-53 Korean War. The minister said the review also includes past responses and mea

item.title: California scientist wins a Nobel Prize, then makes school lunches for his kids
item.description: STANFORD, Calif. — Dr. Karl Deisseroth spent hours fielding congratulatory calls after learning early Monday that he had won a Nobel Prize for medicine for helping to open a new field of brain science called optogenetics. But it wasn't long before the California scientist asked for a break from all the attention for a more ordinary task: He needed to make school lunches for his children, who were asleep in the family home in Stanford, where their father had been speaking in the middle of the night with journalists and well-wishers. Deisseroth, 54, shared this year’s medicine prize with two researchers in Germany for their work in optogenetics, a field that combines light with genes to switch on and off neurons in living brains. A self-described night owl, the Howard Hughes Medical Institute investigator and Stanford University professor often works past midnight. After reviewing papers and emailing his students, he said he had just gone to lie down when he got the call from the Nobel Assembly in Stockholm. “I almost felt as if I’d lost the power of forming words,” he told The A

item.title: What to know about suspected bomb plot against UK air base used by US in Iran war
item.description: LONDON — The U.S. has withdrawn its bombers stationed at a U.S.-run military air base in England used to strike Iran, as police investigate whether a suspected terror plot at the base is linked to Iran. Five men were detained shortly after midnight on Sept. 27 on suspected explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward RAF Fairford. The U.K.-owned base has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including the ongoing Iran war. A sixth suspect, a British-Iranian dual national, was arrested several days later. All the men have been released on bail. Police earlier said they did not find any explosives in the vans that sparked the security alert. The developments have led to confusion about what exactly happened at the air base. British authorities have linked the incident to Tehran. Iran has denied involvement. item.title: 'China has never asked Seoul to choose a side between Beijing, Washington,' envoy says
item.description: As competition between the United States and China increasingly extends from diplomacy to technology and supply chains, Seoul faces the challenge of managing ties with its security ally and one of its most important economic partners. Chinese Ambassador to Korea Dai Bing said Seoul does not need to choose between Washington and Beijing, saying maintaining relations with both countries serves Korea’s national interests. “China has never asked Korea to choose a side between China and the United States,” Dai said in an interview with The Korea Times in Seoul, Sept. 29. “We hope that Korea will pursue sound relations parallel with both China and the United States, guided by its own fundamental national interests.” The ambassador said U.S.-China competition should not be the sole lens through which the regional order in East Asia is viewed, adding China hopes Korea will pursue what he described as “genuine strategic autonomy.” Dai emphasized that strategic autonomy does not mean giving up Korea’s alliance with the U.S., saying China respects the alliance relationship based on
